speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED NEW TREATMENT FOR DRUG ADDICTS
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Has the attention of the minister's department been drawn to a report in the Vancouver Province of June 24, 1961, that success has been achieved in treating drug addicts of between two and 28 years' addiction with a natural substance known as DPN (diphosphopyridine) which has been reported by researcher Dr. Paul O'Hallaren in the United States. If so, is this new development being closely followed in view of the serious drug addiction problem in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monteilh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REPORTED NEW TREATMENT FOR DRUG ADDICTS
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his intention to ask this question. Some days ago the chief of the narcotic control division of my department first heard of the drug mentioned by the hon. member, and immediately wrote to Dr. O'Hallaren in Seattle asking for any information he might be prepared to release covering his research work.
This substance has not been prepared or used in Canada to my knowledge, and I have asked that all possible information on its apparent value be obtained. It would seem that it is used to alleviate withdrawal symptoms when an addict is undergoing treatment for addiction to heroin.

subtopic: SASKATOON
subsubtopic: DISCONTINUANCE OF BENEFITS TO WESTEEL PRODUCTS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. Would the minister explain to the house why employees of Westeel Products of Saskatoon have had their unemployment insurance benefits discontinued even though neither a strike nor a walkout exists; and will the minister take immediate action to bring about a new interpretation of the regulations in regard to this and other like cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: SASKATOON
subsubtopic: DISCONTINUANCE OF BENEFITS TO WESTEEL PRODUCTS EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his intention to ask this question. I want to inform him that this matter was brought to my attention some two weeks ago by the steel workers union, and at that time I asked the commission to undertake an investigation.
I am informed by the unemployment insurance commission that certain personnel were laid off at Westeel and that the management gave, as a reason for the lay-off, "anticipating a strike". Under the circumstances, I am advised that the unemployment office at Saskatoon had no alternative but to disqualify these people.
This is a matter which is covered not by the regulations but by the act itself. Section 63(1) of the Unemployment Insurance Act reads as follows:
An insured person who has lost his employment by reason of a stoppage of work attributable to a

Inquiries of the Ministry
labour dispute at the factory, workshop or other premises at which he was employed, is disqualified from receiving benefit until
(a)	a termination of the stoppage of work,
(b)	he becomes bona fide employed elsewhere in the occupation that he usually follows, or
(c)	he has become regularly engaged in some other occupation, whichever event first occurs.
In view of this I am informed that the officials had no alternative but to disqualify these people and that those laid off have been disqualified as of June 2.

speechtext: I wonder if I might ask the minister whether he would look into the serious consequences of disqualifying people on grounds of an anticipated strike, and if he will consider introducing legislation to amend the act in this regard.

maintopic: HANDLING OF U.S. PUBLICATIONS REMAILED IN CANADA
speechtext: I should like to ask the Postmaster General a question. In view of the United States postal rate increase to 8 cents a pound for United States periodicals mailed to Canada, effective July 1, has the Canadian post office made preparations to handle a huge increase in remailing of United States periodicals in Canada which will take advantage of the much lower Canadian rate on such material?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
maintopic: HANDLING OF U.S. PUBLICATIONS REMAILED IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we do not anticipate any huge increase. The substantial difference in rates will exist only for one month, since our new rate goes into effect on August 1, and it is not the custom for a publisher to make extensive changes in the way of handling his material for one month only.
I might point out that the reason our rate is underneath the United States rate is to compensate for the cost to the publisher of trucking or carrying this material from the United States to the Canadian point where it is placed in the mails. It is of very great interest and benefit to us to have this material placed in the mails in Canada, because if it is placed in the mails in the United States we are obliged to handle it anyway and we get no revenue whatsoever. We therefore established a rate which, together with the cost of transportation, is approximately equivalent to the United States rate thus getting as much revenue as possible.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance took two hours and 40 minutes to deliver his budget speech, and some 37 or 38 minutes yesterday to deliver a further speech on it. Of that fact I have no complaint whatever. I think it was quite proper-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Thirty two minutes, to be exact.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In any event, I think it was quite proper for the minister to do so. The point I wish to make is that I find it somewhat difficult, in the 30 minutes allowed to a private member, to deal thoroughly or adequately with the budget speech. I think the present budget is of such significance to the country that it deserves thorough and analytical examination rather than the shorter, somewhat abrupt treatment that may be given to certain points of it because of the requirement of completing my remarks within 30 minutes. To me it is a matter of regret
The Budget-Mr. Mcllraith that as a private member I do not have more time in which to deal with it as I should like to do.
This budget undoubtedly is significant to the economy of this country. It is of very real significance to the economy of this country this year, and I think a great many of its points have very dangerous implications and are of harmful significance. I should like to be able to analyse my reasons for making that statement in a somewhat more careful way than I will be able to do. Because of the time limit it is going to be necessary to leave out reference to many points I should like to discuss, and it also will be impossible to make a proper analysis of some of the points with which I will try to deal.
There is one thing I should like to point out to the minister before launching into a general discussion of the budget. That is that yesterday in his remarks he made the point that since the budget was delivered the financial markets of this country are stronger than they were before the budget was introduced. The term he used was "the financial markets". I point out to the minister that just last night's newspapers that were on so many desks at the very time he was making that statement, as was pointed out to me at the time-I did not interrupt the minister because I did not wish to consume any of his time-were to the very opposite effect. The Canadian Press story in the Ottawa Journal of yesterday evening was headed "Toronto stocks move downhill". That was supported by a subsidiary story on the Montreal market. The Citizen had a story to the same effect.

That was the one
day.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is the point I wish to make. I trust the minister will bear with me. I tried to be courteous yesterday and not interrupt him because his time was limited. I will try to make my points as clearly as I can. The Montreal Gazette has the same type of story in this morning's issue headed "Market dips again". That is followed by a story headed "Bonds easier". I think what the minister was seeking to deal with was the bond market only and not the financial market generally. I want to point that out

The Budget-Mr. Mcllraith because the other statement is much too wide, as I think an analysis will bear out.
It seemed to me that the budget did not generally represent a well integrated document or program for the economy of this country for the coming year. It seemed to me to be rather a collection, indeed it could probably be called a conglomeration, of contradictory objectives. It is with some of those contradictions that I wish to deal today.
There was one interesting fact that came cut of the minister's presentation. It was the rather startling revelation that the budget had not been prepared in conjunction or with the benefit of discussions with the governor of the Bank of Canada. I do not want to digress into a debate on that matter because there is a bill before the house and it can be discussed fully on another occasion. However I do want to point out that this lack of co-ordination of policies and of the benefit of the experience of that institution is very apparent in this budget. Indeed, from the minister's statement it is apparent that there had been a lack of co-operation and coordination of the Minister of Finance and his department with the Bank of Canada. That, to me, explains many of the inconsistent policies which the minister has revealed in the previous four budgets, and particularly in this one.
I for one got the impression from the minister's statement on that point in his budget speech, and again from his preoccupation last night with the governor of the Bank as opposed to budget matters which had been debated here, that he had been nurturing a grudge. Whether or not he is well justified is another matter which can be debated on the other bill. The point is that the Minister of Finance must assume the responsibility for not attempting to resolve the problem directly. That part of it must surely belong and rest squarely on the minister's shoulders. If the situation was as the minister described it-and those facts have not all been proven yet; they are the subject of controversy- surely the minister owed an obligation to this country to seek to reconcile the governor to his point of view during these last four years.
It is clear from the minister's own words that he was not doing that; and it is clear that had he followed that proper course and the reconciliation could not have been effected, the governor would have had no option but to resign. But to come forward and have the country suffer because the Minister of Finance, for reasons of his own, did not seek to reconcile the governor of the


bank to his views in these matters is something that has sad consequences for the country, and those consequences are reflected in the budget itself.
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of specific comments I wish to make on different aspects of the budget. I think by far the most inadequate portion of the minister's budget speech was the part devoted to international trade and international commercial policies. The minister, it seemed to me, did not develop that subject in the way that was his obligation in the circumstances this country is in at this time with relation to the international trade field. The speech contained no evidence at any point to show that the government realizes the urgency which is required on the part of this country to deal with the revolutionary changes that are taking place today in the field of international trade.
The wording of the speech was so similar to earlier speeches that one would think there had been no changes in that field since 1958. As a matter of fact I compared the objectives in that field which the minister expressed in his 1958 budget speech-those objectives will be found at page 1236 of Hansard of 1958-with the objectives given by the minister in his budget speech of this year, to be found at page 6650 of Hansard. It is rather interesting to find what that comparison shows. In 1958 the minister stated five objectives. In 1961 he lists only three. Upon close reading I discover that the 1961 objectives are in part a summary of the 1958 objectives, but there is one significant difference. I want to point out this significant difference and ask the minister to deal with it at an appropriate stage. I wish to quote two parts of these objectives to point out the difference. In 1958 objective No. 3 read:
To support and promote a regime of law, order and morality in the field of international trade; to respect the spirit and intent of international commitments; and to stand ready to defend our rights and interests if they are challenged or ignored;
In the 1961 budget the same objective reads as follows:
To support and promote a regime of law and order in international trade; to respect our international commitments; and to stand ready to defend our rights and interest.
I wish to point out to hon. members that there are several important differences. I do not intend to make any point of the fact that the minister apparently no longer wishes to support the promotion of a regime of morality in international trade. Of much greater importance, I think, is this point, which I think should be underlined and dealt with by the government on an appropriate occasion. The government apparently no longer intends to

respect the spirit as well as the written content of our international commitments. Perhaps it was an error in drafting; I do not know. If it was, I point out to the government that it is a very substantial error, one which the minister must clarify and one with which he should deal on an appropriate occasion at greater length and with greater care than I am able to deal with it today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I could deal with it now if the hon. member wished. It would only take a moment.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister will surely bear with me. He had ample time in which to deliver his speech, and the house did extend him courtesy in that respect. After all, under our system of government we do discuss and debate these things. I am trying to be strictly relevant to the subject and deal with it as best I can, and surely the minister can abide by the usual rules of conduct in this house.
The minister made much of the use of the exchange fund in dealing with the balance of payments problem and the exchange rate. I point out to him that his remarks in this respect were extremely imprecise. I shall deal further with this matter later. The minister was going to lower the value of the Canadian dollar to an indefinite, unspecified level, and it seems to me that this is contrary to the spirit of the international monetary fund. This is an international agreement which Canada has assumed and which, indeed, we have always been meticulously careful to honour.
It seems to me there is a danger in the failure of the government to speak of the spirit of international commitments for the very good reason that we may be interpreted as not being prepared to live up to the spirit of our commitments in this connection. Indeed, there was a question asked by my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River about what consultations there had been on this point, and the answer was not very clear. Perhaps I can leave that point there. I hope the minister will deal with it fully on an appropriate occasion, because it could have important international implications particularly since our reputation in this field generally has been good, and one of which Canadians are proud.
Before elaborating on this question of international trade I should like to say one thing. It seems to me to be basic that before deciding on any policy there must be a clear analysis of the problem. This step must underlie any successful policy. To act on any other basis or to act on the basis of an inadequate analysis means that the policy itself
The Budget-Mr. Mcllraith will be erroneous and inadequate. I believe the minister would agree with me in this respect.
The point I wish to emphasize in relation to this field of international trade is that it seems to me the minister has failed altogether to appreciate the underlying problem. He has failed to make a competent or thorough analysis of the situation. He has failed to pay sufficient attention to the trend toward regional blocs, a trend which may, in many respects, be outside our control, but which nevertheless should not simply be ignored for that reason. There can be no adequate policy developed for Canada unless there is a recognition of what is going on.
I could elaborate a great deal, but it seems to me that in his budget the hon. gentleman has failed to take into account the developments taking place in connection with the European common market. He has failed to recognize the progressive and continuous movement of the outer seven into closer relationship with the European common market group. The minister will have noticed further news items on this very point in today's press. It seems to me that in dealing with our relationship to Great Britain the hon. gentleman has not adapted his mind to the fact that Britain may very well seek to move into the common market. I am not proposing to debate at this time whether she should or should not do so, because that is a matter which will be determined by the United Kingdom and it is not my intention to encroach upon decisions which must remain hers, but we have a very close interest in the subject. The minister's attitude has been in the nature of threats of retaliatory action if they take such a step.

speechtext:
My views on this subject were advanced in an earlier debate on April 24 and 25, on one of the supply motions. Perhaps I could leave them now without further elaboration. But there must surely be in this country a greater appreciation of these developments which are taking place, and an attempt to bring ourselves into a better relationship with the facts as they exist. This may involve our having to make some changes.
The minister made no reference at all to the Latin American free trade area which came into effect a few weeks ago. The whole subject is dealt with in the Montevideo treaty. That is something which should be acknowledged and it must be considered when policy is set for the future of this country. It is true that our dollar trade in that area last year was relatively small. I think our exports last year were of the order of $100 million. But

The Budget-Mr. Mcllraith the potential there is something which cannot be ignored, and this is certainly a bloc with a very large population. There is every indication that there may be a rapidly developing economy in that area.
It seems to me the minister's policy approach in this direction is completely inadequate. The hon. gentleman has ignored the situation. Indeed, in an earlier debate on the subject of trade I accused him of making speeches which were of a threatening nature, and I sought on that occasion to quote many items in support of my assertion. It seems to me that the same weakness is in his budget speech. It is not satisfactory, and for my part I think there must be a complete new examination and a movement forward to a more constructive position in our own self interest.
We have put forward a program. My leader did it particularly well in the debate to which I have referred and on several other occasions, so perhaps I need not restate the principles which we believe should be asserted in bringing ourselves into better alignment with these trade movements which are coming about in Europe. If we fail to do this, then the unemployment problem, which is a very real problem in Canada, will not be solved. It seems to me that the government has taken no step toward the solution of our trade difficulties in this respect.
Now I wish to turn to another subject, namely the minister's reference in his budget speech to the adjustment of the exchange rate. The minister proposes to use the exchange fund to add substantial amounts to its holdings of United States dollars through purchases in the exchange market. I wish to quote the minister precisely on that point. In dealing with the subject he said "It may well be appropriate for it"-that is, the exchange rate-"to move to a significant discount". That was the language he used. Then in a totally inadequate way he made the bald assertion that the decline in the exchange rate would mean modest price advances. In another place he said the price advances would be minimal. I believe those were the minister's exact words.
In his remarks yesterday the hon. gentleman sought to deal with the Liberal position on this issue. I think he did himself a great injustice in the quotations he used, because if he had taken the trouble to closely examine those quotations he would have seen they were dealing with the artificially high exchange rate in an attempt to reduce it from an artificially high level. I think all hon. members will agree that the balance of payments problem has been and is a very real one in Canada, and that our high exchange rate should be reduced; but that is not what the minister said in his budget speech. He

did not take that line at all. He said that it may well be appropriate for it to move to a significant discount.
Hon. members will notice the looseness of language. The minister referred to "a significant discount", but did not say what was a significant discount. Did he have reference to the Canadian dollar being below the value of the United States dollar by the former rate of 20 per cent? Did he mean 10 per cent, 5 per cent, 2 per cent or 1 per cent? That kind of imprecision is not good enough for a minister of finance in dealing with this difficult and important subject. That kind of handling of this subject may have very serious effects on the economy of this country. The minister did not deal with this problem in a well integrated way.
The minister went on to say he was going to use the exchange fund, which I understand has about $1.8 billion or more of United States dollars. That is to say, the Canadian taxpayers have about that amount of United States dollars held in that account. Is he going to add to it? What amount will he add? What are the financial implications of that part of his speech? Did he take the financial implications into account in fixing his estimate of the deficit for this year? What is the minister's attitude on that? Nothing was said. Is it any wonder that there is uneasiness in the financial markets of this country? Is it any wonder that there is in those markets criticism of the minister's imprecision?
It is quite true that bringing down the Canadian dollar from its high level will give an admitted temporary advantage to our export industries. I think anyone would agree that that is desirable. I am sure there is no quarrel with that. But that desirable effect must be weighed against the consequences of what the minister has done in this budget by his attempt to bring down the exchange rate to an undefined significant discount. You will notice he is using the phrase "significant discount", and you take your choice as to what it means. The consequences of doing so may be very adverse to this country. It is that kind of looseness on the part of the minister in dealing with this important subject that caused me at the opening of my remarks to deplore the lack of a well integrated statement on the part of the minister, and the lack of the benefit of the experience of the Bank of Canada in the preparation of the budget.
Let me point out some of the adverse things that must be taken into consideration if the minister succeeds in bringing down the dollar, not to par but to a significant discount. Undoubtedly our cost of living will

increase. I was rather shocked that the minister should have dismissed that subject so lightly. It is rather elementary. If you take the volume of imports to this country and consider that some are consumer goods, some are raw materials and some are semi-finished materials going into production, it means an increase in the cost of living. There was no assessment of that counterbalancing problem on the part of the minister. There was no attempt on his part to exercise the judgment and care that should be exercised on this subject so the problem could be dealt with in a way that would not have led to our backing into a worse and more destructive problem.
We must remember that this cost of living increase is coming at a time when the Ontario provincial government is placing a tax of 3 per cent on the sale of practically all goods. When one bears in mind the importance of Ontario to the economy of Canada in terms of population, productive capacity and so on, one can readily see how significant the cost of living increase may be this year at a time when we have a high level of unemployment and much unused capacity. The minister has not dealt with that in a thorough way in his budget.
The minister said he was going to reduce interest rates. That was an interesting statement to come from the minister who did so much to start the increase in interest rates, especially as a result of his mishandling of the conversion loan of 1958. First the interest rates were forced up as a result of his mishandling of that loan. He forced municipal borrowers and many corporate borrowers to go to the United States for their borrowings. If the minister succeeds in achieving a significant discount on our dollar he will force the municipal borrowers to pay a premium on their interest charges in the United States after having initially created the problem for them. He will place an added burden on the municipalities and corporations.
What is the minister's analysis of that problem in his budget speech? I simply do not find it. He simply said he is going to reduce interest charges. He did not tell us what impact his billion dollar borrowings this year would have on interest rates. Can one be blamed for suspecting that the implication of that is that it will tend to increase interest rates rather than lower them? I may be naive, but I thought the federal government going into the markets of this country and borrowing a billion dollars this year would lessen the money available for investment in corporation, municipal and provincial securities, and that it would have created 90205-6-457
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell considerable pressure to raise interest rates. But, no; the minister did not see fit to deal with that problem at all.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman is going to use the printing presses.

Unfortunately that is what I am beginning to suspect. In any event, let me deal with another aspect of it.
The minister is concerned about that problem also. If he is truly concerned, why did he not in his budget deal with the consequences of bringing down the value of the Canadian dollar from its artificially high level not to par but to a significant discount? What effect will that have on United States investment in Canada? It will mean that investment in Canada will be more enticing to United States investors because with $100 of United States money American investors can purchase a larger share of ownership and more securities than they could purchase before the exchange rate was brought down to this significant discount. That is a problem that should be carefully analysed, and I regret that time does not permit me to do so. The minister has not dealt with these things which are inherent in this budget. These are the inconsistencies that show up in the budget.
I wanted to speak about one other thing. The minister said yesterday that we had not put forward positive recommendations. We have put forward positive recommendations as to what should be done to get us out of the economic difficulty in which we find ourselves. We put forward many matters that are strictly budgetary, on April 25 at page 3985 of Hansard and on May 3 at page 3402.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have a chance to speak briefly in this budget debate for two reasons. First of all, no one will deny that it is an important budget. One has only to look at the things pending in the world, so to speak, such as Britain's trading relation with Europe, our own attitude toward the organization of American states, and the question of aid to underdeveloped countries, as well as other problems. That is one reason I am glad to speak. The other is that I am glad to be speaking because I have an old relationship and friendship with the Minister of Finance and if I can do anything, however small, to help him on his way I am glad to do it. He
7238	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell and I shared a room here for four years. Of course many hon. members will sympathize with both of us for that reason, but we managed to come through it pretty well unscathed.
In my opinion the minister has been very realistic in what he has said, and I want to try to act in the same way. I am not going to deal with the points he dealt with yesterday, the questions of exchange, the deficit, the interest rate, particularly vis-a-vis the opposition, because I think he handled them adequately. I want to say just one word about what the hon. member for Ottawa West has been saying, namely the suggestion that the minister had not been sufficiently concerned with external trade, but that somehow that was being neglected. In that connection I suggest that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have really beaten a path to all kinds of discussions of this broad and important question, both in Europe and in the United States. I feel that any suggestion that it is being ignored or dealt with carelessly just does not click.
My anxiety today is to try to sense public opinion particularly as indicated by the press. In doing that it is useful to see what the enemy is saying. I have looked at those newspapers which we usually find taking the other side. Naturally I went first of all to the Winnipeg Free Press. One can always be sure that in the case of the Winnipeg Free Press, to adopt the words they used to use in the air force, we will get "loud and clear" expression of what they have to say, particularly in that left-hand column with which we are all so familiar. I was not disappointed. I found a couple of typical phrases. I imagine these phrases are probably in what I could call the cliche morgue. We know there is a morgue for photographs. They have them on hand when people die, and I imagine there is a morgue for cliches as well, and in a sense you pick them out perhaps with the help of a card index.
I found a couple of the usual things. First of all I found that the budget was motivated by "desperation and political expediency" and that "the government had decided to exert open and partisan political influence over the economy". Well, there you are. That is exactly what you would expect, and one would be disappointed if the Winnipeg Free Press did not come up with something like that. My feeling about that is that it can be answered in the words of the English yokel who was insulted by one of his friends. He passed it off by saying "It pleases he and it don't hurt I". I feel that is the attitude one can take toward that indomitable left-hand column of the Winnipeg Free Press.


However, there was a contributed editorial by one signing himself "M.W.". It was not in the sacred left-hand column, it was in the middle. I was really quite astonished because common sense seemed to creep in there, and some things were said which I thought the writer would hardly dare to say. Let me quote just a few words. He said:
The budget offers various new incentives to Canadian industry to undertake re-equipment, modernization of plant and greater research activity in Canada. These are important but like many of the other changes too detailed for consideration here.
It struck me that that was rather typical. When you come to good things they are "too detailed"; the good things done by this government are too detailed for much consideration in the Winnipeg Free Press.
I go back now to the left-hand column. We had, of course, the usual diatribe about high tariffs, entirely ignoring the loyalty which this government has shown to GATT and to the aims of increasing world trade. But again I say we must not take it too seriously. We must understand; we must realize that they just cannot help it, that they are born that way and these things have to be said. They are still living in the atmosphere of 1911, the time of the reciprocity campaign.
I come next to the Toronto Star, and really something happened that I would not have believed possible. I find myself sympathizing with the Toronto Star. I never thought I could do that. But when I found that in a short editorial they were forced to use words of approval of the Minister of Finance I said to myself these are new days. For the Toronto Star perhaps they are sad days, but they welcomed devaluation and lower interest rates. Of course they covered themselves by saying it was just their own idea which the Minister of Finance had copied. They went on to say that this should "stimulate business considerably".
Of course they had a complaint. The complaint was that the Minister of Finance is "not sure how far and how fast he must go". Well I am quite sure that the Star-and I apply this also to the hon. member for Ottawa West-does not have the idea that the minister is going now to give a lot of figures and tell us just exactly what is going to happen. That surely is not within the realm of common sense. No sane man would suggest that. It has to depend on the march of events, and the minister put it extremely well. He said "Our objective is to achieve an exchange rate which will contribute to a better balance in our current account position." That is common sense, and no common sense man would want to do more than that.

I come for a moment to the Globe and Mail, which in my opinion bravely tries to steer a middle course between the respective traditions of its progenitors, the Grit Globe and the Tory Mail and Empire. While they criticize the minister for failing to reduce taxes, they have some general words of approval which I would like to quote because they have some interesting implications. The Globe and Mail says:
The public may have been led to expect a major fiscal miracle from Mr. Fleming because the other political parties have not hesitated to assert that, placed in power, they would engage in that kind of hocus-pocus. It should be remembered that these political aspirants base their promises upon two false premises. One, is that Canada is in a hopeless economic condition;-
That is the Liberals. I continue:
-the other, is that the system which has given us the second highest level of prosperity in the world is a worthless system and ought to be scrapped.
I continue to quote from the Globe and Mail:
Mr. Fleming approached his budget in the belief, which we share, that Canada is not a ruined country, although it is in difficulties. He justly pointed out that we still have vast natural resources and talent which can be put to constructive wealth creating use. Equally, he held to the belief that on the whole the system of free enterprise and free competition offers the best chance for our progress.
I have quoted that because the Globe and Mail has taken the position I want to take of applauding the minister because he has not believed in miracles but rather has believed in patience, detailed discussion of problems, and dealing with them one by one. As I said, the Globe and Mail did criticize the minister because he did not lower high taxes. My answer to that is that the minister was facing huge expenditures, largely inherited and resulting in a large deficit, and that he might well hesitate to increase this by further large decreases in taxation which might have an inflationary effect. That satisfies me and I think it would satisfy the ordinary sensible person.
I want to say a few words at this point about the course of economic events since the war. There is no mystery about what has seen happening. We had a boom for more ;han ten years. I think the Hamilton Spectator described this period admirably when it said in its issue of June 21:
In the post-war years when Canada had everything its own way, when a rebuilding Europe and a bursting economy at home had us in the seller's pulpit, with buyers at almost any price we cared to ask, the Liberal government of the day put up massive ... spending levels.
I think that is true, and I do not know that I am saying it particularly critically.
90205-6-4574
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell They had the revenue and they were tempted to spend it. At first we did not realize that this boom was coming after the war. We were very apprehensive that things might be very flat, and it is interesting to note that at that time, not realizing the boom that was coming, not realizing that the flames were going to be burning pretty brightly anyway, we fanned the flames in a quite substantial way by a loan of a billion and a quarter to Great Britain, which we approved. I made a speech in favour of it myself.
It is interesting to remember that the loan was put before the House of Commons by Mr. Ilsley, the minister of that day, really on the basis of two main arguments. The first was that Britain, who had borne the burden and heat of the day and had divested herself of many of her investments, was entitled to assistance if anyone ever was. Second, and just as important, he pointed out that this was in our own interests, that our external trade greatly needed to be built up, that Britain was unable to be a purchaser, and and that therefore it was highly in our own interests to make them advances so they could buy. It was really just like a wholesaler who assists an important customer who for the moment is broke. That was the argument which was made. That money was spent here and, as I say, it fanned the flames and, as the Hamilton Spectator said, we really had it all our own way. It would not have been human if we had not taken advantage of it but, mark you, it left a situation which we ought to look at very carefully and try to understand now.
A little later, of course, we had the Korean episode which again fanned the flames and incidentally, of course, at that time the cost of living was going up very rapidly. Between 1945 and 1952 the cost of living went up by about 50 per cent. In 1945 the consumer price index, on the basis of 1949 equalling 100, stood at 75 and in 1952 it was 116.5. It was inevitable that this should happen. I am not criticizing it particularly; I am just pointing out the situation. I want to try to be realistic as I think the minister was realistic. I think we have got serious problems and we ought to face them like serious men. We can never face them if we do not know what they are.
As I say, there is no mystery about what has happened since. That gorgeous period pretty well came to an end in 1955 or 1956. I say there is no mystery about what has happened since. The boom came to an end. One strange thing about booms is that people always think they are going to go on forever but they never do go on forever. The boom came to an end. It did not come to an
7240	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell end with a terrific flop; it came to an end rather quietly. Things flattened out rather than having a tremendous fall.
At the same time two other terribly important things happened. The competition of western Europe came into the picture in a big way. We all know what that meant. Western Europe had been given a flying start by the Marshall plan. I was reading just last night about General Marshall and the Marshall plan. We owe a great deal to that very great man for the courage he showed. But what did it mean? It meant that western Europe had new machinery, new methods and, as I say, was given a flying start. More than that, and this is the thing we should all be registering in this country of ours, they not only had a healthy and skilled industrial class but in some way they managed to make the industrial class feel they were working for themselves. There was a better relationship between employer and employee. I fear we must admit that is so, and if it is true we should register it and seriously consider it. I fear it is true that they had and still have a better relationship, partly because of the laws, between employer and employee. These men realized, as I say, that they were working for themselves, and as a result western Europe has become a formidable competitor in the foreign trade market. This is something we cannot laugh off. One of the things I give the minister credit for is that he is telling us this faithfully and straightly and trying to make us realize that it depends on ourselves to pull up our socks, that it cannot all be done by government.
At the same time we should not forget that Japan has been revitalized and is a great competitor, as we know; that the communist countries, whenever it suits them, can sell at prices which have no relation to cost, and that the United States too is pulling up its socks. There is a danger, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has warned people, that a softening process has gone on. The minister compared us to a boxer-he was once a boxer himself-who has gone soft and feels that there is no real reason for special effort. We have reached the stage now when there is a reason for special effort, and the minister has tried to impress that on us.
There is another thing which has happened which affects the situation and is a commonplace to us all, of course. I am referring now particularly to unemployment and the effect of automation. There is also the movement of people from the land to the cities resulting in a decline in the agricultural population. The bright lights are more attractive and, of course, new and improved farm machinery means that a machine can produce as much


food as 20 or 30 men and such machines have taken the place of those who have left the farm.
There is one other thing I should like to mention in passing. There has been quite a lot of talk about a $2 billion deficit over four years. I should like to put on the record the figures as to increased expenditure since the government came into power, nearly all inherited. There has been a rise each year from 1957-58 to 1960-61 over the expenditure of the preceding year, and in the four years the total increase has been $2,719 million of added burdens that the minister has had to carry. It is not very surprising that there has been a deficit.
I said that I thought the minister had been realistic, and I should like to say briefly what I mean by that. He has resisted the idea that we can cure the situation by bookkeeping or by tariff tricks. The minister has refused showy and quick remedies. He seems to me like a man who is trying to build a solid structure and not a jerry-built affair which in a few years we might find cracking and letting us down. I think he has been courageous and wise in what he has done, and I believe that the course of events will prove the value of his decision.
He is not hesitating to accept new ideas, particularly in connection with the matter of exchange. Incidentally, in that connection it is fashionable now to suggest that the minister has changed his mind. All right. It is only people of stature who can change their minds. I like a quotation which I ran across the other day from Joseph Chamberlain, the father of Neville, who was a great figure 50 years ago. Somebody charged him once with having changed his mind. He said "Anyone is welcome to my discarded opinions". I think that is a very good comment on the idea that a man must never change his mind as circumstances change.
As I said a moment ago, the minister has not pretended that governments by tariff or bookkeeping tricks can deal wholly with the situation or bring the economy back to a satisfactory position. He has in plain terms left this burden where it belongs, namely on the energy, capacity and, if necessary, the sacrifice of Canadian citizens. Yes, that is what the President of the United States put up to the Americans, namely sacrifice if necessary. He has had no part in what the Globe and Mail calls hocus-pocus. He is helping people to help themselves.
Let us consider a few of the things which the Free Press did not have time to mention. First of all there is the substantial extension of the powers of the industrial development bank. That is an important matter. It can help

a great deal. It can help people who could not get credit previously. Its powers are being extended. There was a time when credit could be given by the bank only when it had been refused elsewhere.
Let us also consider other things which the Free Press had not time to mention. There are the tax incentives to stimulate scientific research; double depreciation, the 50 per cent increase in the rates of capital cost allowance applicable to new assets. These are only a few of the array of things which the budget brought in. What I like about them is that each one of them appears to me to be a sound contribution to assist the economy. They all seem to me to be things which have been investigated, studied and assessed having regard to the value they can be to the economy. The matter cannot be better put than in the way it was put by the minister in his speech. As found at page 6642 of Hansard he said this:
I need not remind hon. members that there is no royal road, no magic which a minister of finance may invoke to achieve these goals. If there were easy solutions they would have been adopted long ago.
How true that statement is.
Nor can these objectives be attained by federal government measures alone. In our free enterprise system we shall need self-discipline and the full co-operation of business, labour and all levels of government-indeed of all our people-if we are to succeed.
Those are the minister's words, and I do not think the matter could be better put. There is no hocus-pocus as the Globe and Mail said. There is no claim of magic power on the part of government. However, there is reference to self-discipline, co-operation, courage and caution. Surely this is the kind of language and the kind of action that serious people like ourselves are entitled to expect from the government.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the philosophical apologia given by our highly respected friend1 the hon. member for Greenwood. I was greatly interested to note that he recognized the international aspects of our economic problems. I think we all must recognize them. There are certain factors over which we have little or no control, and which make our problems more complicated and serious today than they have possibly ever been in world history.
The hon. member made some reference to the editorial writer of the Free Press sloughing over the details of some of the good things in the budget. While I do not blame the hon. gentleman for highlighting them to the best
The Budget-Mr. Herridge of his ability, may I say that possibly the editor on that ocasion failed to have a microscope with him.
The hon. member mentioned our vast resources in this country. We are not a finished or a poor people. I am sure no members of this house think Canada is in a state of ruin, particularly when we all realize that we have the vast resources mentioned by the hon. gentleman which can be developed over a period of many years. We also have a virile and industrious people who can apply their energy to the development of these resources. We in this group are also very much concerned with the fact that we have hundreds of thousands of working people in Canada who are anxious to have that opportunity.
The hon. gentleman also mentioned the afterwar boom period, and rightly so. One of the fundamental approaches that we take to economic problems is with regard to this continuing boom and bust in capitalist society. We think that the application of human intelligence and a spirit of co-operation can remedy the boom and bust society with its consequent insecurity for large numbers of good people.
The minister delivered what I think has been quite correctly termed his marathon speech with his usual Cromwellian stance and stentorian voice. I always watch the minister with great interest, and I give him full marks for his courage and bold front under economic adversity. I always admire a person who stands up for his convictions and defends what he believes to be the right course. However, I think it is quite fair to say it is obvious that he has changed his direction considerably since the last budget. There are many contradictions in the minister's statements and direction since 1957 which reflect-and I have some sympathy with the minister on this account-the vacillations and uncertainties of the capitalist system under which we live. In my opinion the budget is a sincere attempt on the part of the minister to rationalize the conflict between capitalist interests in Canada, the circumstances that prevail in the country and the politcal necessities of the party in power. I think without a doubt he has done his best to that end, and we give him full marks in that direction.
Mr. Speaker, we are the only group in this house that offers a completely alternative program to meet the necessities of our times.

As a sort of prelude to what I have to say later on I wish to read two paragraphs from his book dealing with this particular question of socialism versus capitalism:
Sound democratic socialism will seek public ownership under democratic control of the commanding heights of the modern economic order. There is no need for that.
There is a wholesome stimulus in competition, or emulation, and in diversity of functional apparatus.

Public ownership need not be of one type. Generally speaking, the state should be the agency of ownership, and public corporations or authorities of somewhat various types its administrators. But there will be a large place for co-operatives, especially consumers' cooperatives, in the good society.
I read that quotation, Mr. Speaker, because I think it indicates very well the economic philosophy of this group which we have mentioned previously in the house on numerous occasions. It is the mixed economy or dual economy operated for the welfare of the people as a whole and not for the few.

Mr. Fleming's gamble

speechtext: What would the hon. member propose to do in the face of this situation, where we are faced with a deficit of $650 million as a result of various measures of which the hon. member is aware? subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was just coming to that; the minister anticipated my solution. In our opinion the deficit could be considerably reduced. In our opinion corporations are still being allowed to retain too large a slice of their profits under these circumstances when we relate their profits to the situation throughout the country with regard to unemployment. Therefore we believe that this deficit could have been considerably reduced by an increase in corporation taxes and by a reduction of depletion allowances in particular circumstances with respect to certain companies where in our opinion this measure is considerably abused; also by the reduction of depreciation allowances under certain circumstances. We are quite in agreement with the minister's attempt to assist small industry and the development of industry with depletion allowances and depreciation allowances, but we are of the opinion that these allowances under the Income Tax Act are being very much abused in some quarters and that with an increase in these taxes we could
The Budget-Mr. Herridge have considerably reduced the present deficit. The minister may not agree with us, but that is what we believe.
In addition we must remember that when it comes to the question of income tax, the only persons in Canada when the government can be certain will meet their income tax obligations in full are employees whose income tax is deducted at the source, or farmers selling through recognized marketing organizations. I have some knowledge of business, and on certain occasions I have been appalled to find out what can be done under the income tax regulations. I think we are particularly generous in that respect.
As socialists I think it is only fair that we should offer alternatives to the present budget proposals, and we do that. We believe we are justified in incurring a large scale deficit as the result of investment in self liquidating, publicly owned projects, which would provide for co-operation in financing provincial projects and an extension of such programs as the winter works program. We believe it is quite sound to go into debt on capital investment in self-liquidating projects because the investment is there to equate the expenditure.
Then we believe there should be a planned program of production to assist the Asian, African and Latin American countries, financed in a way very similar to the way the war production program was financed. We believe this is a serious situation and that we can do something to improve our own domestic economic situation and at the same time accept our responsibilities to an even greater extent to other countries abroad. We believe investment in this field is very sound and will prove a good investment in the present world situation.
We believe in increased capital in the industrial development bank to provide long term loans to medium and small sized industry and business. The minister is providing for that to some extent in his budget. However, we say there should be provision in the loan to the medium or small sized industry for the state to become a partner in such industry or business, or the companies concerned having an opportunity for repayment of the loans in question.
I for one recognize that two and two make four. I do not underestimate the difficulties we face today, but we believe that if we could develop a program of this sort based on planned fiscal development and investment policies which would also require, in my opinion, a revolution with regard to our sense of values, the future would be much brighter than it appears to be today. Of course
7244	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Herridge these are the things which restrict governments; you cannot move faster than you can obtain a large measure of public support for a project. But we believe that a program of this type with further extensions, as a result of co-operation among provincial, dominion and municipal governments, cooperation with labour, co-operation with agriculture and even co-operation with socially responsible industry and business in this country-and there are large segments of our industry and business which are socially responsible-would lead to results such as our present policies could scarcely hope to achieve. We can implement a program with desirable national objectives under national direction and with a national purpose-that is a very necessary thing-which would provide the same support for the government and for the program that governments receive during wartime.
I am convinced, and so is the party to which I belong, that we must launch out in another direction. We can mobilize support for a program designed to serve the people and controlled by the people, having long term objectives such as I have mentioned. We do not suggest for a moment that all our ills, economic and social, can be cured overnight, but let us change our direction; let us get on a course which can bring results of the type we desire.
We have some examples to guide us. Go to Sweden. Go to Norway, where with far less natural resources than our own and far less opportunities for a program of this kind some marvellous things have been achieved.
I will admit this, that in those countries there is a co-operative philosophy existing among the people, even among the industrialists, which does not exist in this country at the present time. We believe it is up to the national government to give some leadership in this respect. We believe that if we could once change our course, change our direction, we could offer a hope; we could give a purpose to life in Canada, and we could start to march along the road to stability in our economy and basic security for all who are willing to do their share toward this end.
Having made those few remarks with respect to our general approach, I wish to deal with a few of the good features in the budget. We in this group were very glad to hear the minister repeal the excise tax of per cent on passenger cars. This will be welcomed by many people and will be of some assistance to the automobile industry and the employees engaged therein. It is a worth-while poultice on the ills of society.

I suggest that in my opinion this section of the budget would not stand close scutiny as against the terms of the bill of rights. I bring that to the minister's attention.

The Budget-Mr. Herridge
There is a mild tonic in the budget to which I should like to refer. The minister proposes an increase in the lending resources of the industrial development bank from $160 million to $400 million. We support this proposal wholeheartedly and believe it should be of some assistance to the economy if handled properly. I say that, Mr. Speaker, because I have known of one instance in which a corporation owned and controlled in the United States but located in my constituency was able to obtain quite a large loan, while quite a number of smaller Canadian owned companies were not able to take advantage of this act. As I mentioned before, we believe there is an opportunity here for the granting of loans on the basis that the owners of industries are willing to permit the government to become partners in those industries, or they can agree to full repayment of the loan. I believe this provision is worthy of some consideration in view of what has been done in Scandinavian countries in this respect.
I see the minister proposes a clinical examination of our financial structure and institutions, including the Bank of Canada. I think this is a most interesting proposal and has considerable merit. However, I suggest that the terms of reference of the royal commission should be wide enough to permit an examination of similar institutions in European countries, and I am thinking particularly of the Scandinavian countries and some western European countries in which they have had great success in relating monetary, fiscal and economic policies to the advantage of the country concerned.
Now, I have a few suggestions which I consider would improve the present budget. This budget does not provide for any change in personal income taxes. I am of the opinion that consideration should have been given to increasing the exemptions for persons in lower income groups. I believe provision should be made also for exemption of travelling expenses incurred by workers living at some distance from their employment. These monthly expenses can be quite large. Owing to the difficulty of obtaining housing, as well as other circumstances, you find workers living at increasingly greater distances from their place of employment, sometimes up to 25 or 30 miles in my own constituency. As a result they incur heavy travelling expenses.
I have mentioned this in years past, and I have no hesitation in mentioning it again. I believe these workers should be permitted some exemption in respect of these travelling expenses, particularly when we realize the frivolous expenditures that can be included as travelling expenses by travellers for certain
7246	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Hon. P. Martin companies. I have been told of an instance in which a man travelled 100 miles to sell bubble gum, at least that was the pretext upon which the journey was made, and his expenses were allowed in respect of income tax because he worked for a wholesale grocer.
In view of the depreciation allowed mining companies and companies developing oil and gas wells, I say the same consideration should be given to farmers who use their capital or borrow money to bring land into production by clearing, by irrigation or by draining. The whole theory behind depreciation allowances with respect to those mining and oil and gas companies is that they are increasing the productivity of the country, they are adding to the total production. Farmers should be treated in exactly the same way. The farmer who brings land into production should have the opportunity to claim an exemption for the cost of that development. Similar consideration should be given to persons engaged in the conservation and protection of forest resources by the construction of roads, telephone lines and the purchase of equipment for fire protection and efforts taken to overcome destruction by insects and disease.

This morning I asked the Minister of Finance when the house might expect the government to deal with the recommendations contained in the royal commission report on the automotive industry. The minister's reply was inconclusive. I am sure I can say his reply will be received in the community from which I come with very much regret. I say this because of the dominion bureau of statistics figures regarding the sales of motor vehicles in this country which were given out on June 27. This report shows that in the month of May the shipment of Canadian made motor vehicles declined 4.8 per cent; that is to say, declined to 41,234 units from 43,334 in the corresponding month last year. The report also revealed that shipments of passenger cars in May fell by 5 per cent. In the same month the shipment of commercial vehicles dropped 3.9 per cent.
I believe these figures reveal the considerable urgency and desirability of the government giving immediate consideration to the recommendations of the Bladen royal commission. The royal commission was appointed over a year ago. The government has had the report for some time now. Requests were made by me on several occasions prior to the budget


for an opportunity to peruse the report. However, the government withheld it until the presentation of the budget.
An examination of the royal commission report does not reveal that it contained anything of a character that could not be revealed, unless the government takes the position that the acceptance of the first recommendation, for the elimination of excise tax, was a matter so confidential as to preclude hon. members from seeing the terms of the report. In any event, I suggest that the figures I have just mentioned with regard to the drop in automobile production, together with the decrease in previous months, leave shipments in the January-May period almost 15 per cent below those of a year ago. I believe those figures are such as to warrant a more immediate confrontation by the government of the royal commission report on the automobile industry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At the end of my
time I shall be glad to answer questions. I regret to think that the report of the Bladen commission is to suffer the fate of the reports of so many other royal commissions appointed by this government. We have had many commissions, such as the O'Leary commission and the royal commission dealing with medical care services announced last December 18 which is only now receiving its full complement of personnel as the result of a decision made about two weeks ago. Now we have a further suggestion by the Minister of Finance of a royal commission on monetary, fiscal and financial matters.
I do not want to digress from the main theme of what I have to say today, but with regard to the proposed royal commission on monetary matters I would simply say that the Bank of Canada Act in this country is so similar to the corresponding legislative provision in the United Kingdom that we might well have profited from the royal commission headed by Lord Radcliffe in the United Kingdom. In any event, much of the work of the proposed commission might well have been performed by a committee of this house. I hope that the fate of those commissions, including the Bladen commission, will not come within the mischief of the attack on the principle of royal commissions by Mr. Alan Herbert, M.P., who spoke of the futility of royal commissions in the United Kingdom a few years ago. Here is what he said:
I am sure that the financial secretary will get this vote without any difficulty, but I should like some asurance that this money is not going to be wasted, as the money spent upon royal commissions is, I do not think it is putting it too high, to say nearly always wasted. I am probably the only

member of this committee who in his election address boldly asserted that when he became a member of parliament he would set his face against the habit of government departments asking royal commissions to find out things which they ought to know already themselves, and which almost everybody else knows. Therefore, I am bound to make my protest now. A royal commission is generally appointed, not so much for digging up the truth, as for digging it in and a government department appointing a royal commission is like a dog burying a bone, except that the dog does eventually return to the bone. In my short experience of royal commission I find that they spend perhaps years going into a question, that public-spirited ladies and gentlemen give their services free in doing that work, that they produce portentous and expensively-printed reports and that nothing happens.
This is a serious indictment on royal commissions, and what Mr. Herbert has said applies for the most part to royal commissions appointed by this government. In my community of Windsor and in places such as Oshawa, St. Catharines, Oakville and other industrial communities of our country there was great expectation from the setting up of the Bladen royal commission. Now, however, a year after its appointment, we are no further advanced with regard to solutions to meet the conditions which prevail in the automotive industry. Because of the reply we had this morning to my question to the Minister of Finance, and from the way in which the Bladen commission report was so carelesly passed over in the budget, 1 am afraid that the report of this commission will suffer the same fate as that of other royal commissions appointed by this government.
It should be clearly understood that the initiative for this commission was not taken by this government; it was taken by the communities concerned, namely Windsor and adjoining communities whose economies are so closely tied to the domestic manufacture of motor vehicles and parts, places such as St. Catharines, Oshawa, Oakville and other industrial centres of our country. I may say on this point that a number of individuals might well be mentioned as having taken the lead in impressing on the government the importance of an objective and thorough study of the problems of the automotive industry. But generally speaking the impetus came from those communities themselves, from municipal leaders, from workers, social welfare agencies and business. It is true that the unions and the automotive companies co-operated to the fullest extent, but I want to emphasize that the royal commission hearing finally granted by the government came about as the result of a popular and broadly based demand by the people of these communities whose present and future are so dependent on a healthy motor vehicle industry in Canada.

The Budget-Hon. P. Martin
Among the bodies which made a contribution to the setting up of the commission was the greater Windsor industrial commission, a body that appeared before the Prime Minister in June of 1960. That body pointed out, among other things, that imports of automobile parts in 1959 increased 20 per cent over 1958; that imports of automobile parts in 1959 reached a new high of $319 million; that the United States supplied over 96 per cent of those parts; that imports of completed units in 1959 increased 46 per cent over the previous year; that imports of completed units in 1959 increased 105 per cent over all but one of the preceding years, that the United Kingdom supplied 47.5 per cent of the passenger units in 1959; that West Germany supplied 23.5 per cent of the passenger units in 1959, and imported passenger units from the United Kingdom increased 52 per cent in 1959 over the previous year.
It was as the result of submissions like that from the greater Windsor industrial commission, supported by the mayor of the city of Windsor and the mayors of the adjoining municipalities and the bodies I have mentioned, that the stimulation grew for the establishment of this royal commission. That we should be no further ahead now is a matter of great regret to the community from which I come.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the excise tax?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am going to deal with the excise tax which was promised-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At the end of my
speech. I only have half an hour and I want to cover this matter. The excise tax was removed only the other day as a result of representations made by opposition members, notwithstanding the promise made by the Prime Minister on at least two occasions, in the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958 when he promised that the excise tax on automobiles would be eliminated, not just partially but completely right away, not four years later.
I say to the minister that he has had an opportunity to examine the Bladen report, and he should have been in a position to tell us on behalf of the government what portions of that report were acceptable to the government. Instead we have this further delay in the face of the situation which now confronts the automobile industry, as indicated by the statistics I have thus far put on the record.
The acceptance of the proposal for the elimination of the excise tax of 7J per cent was very welcome. I have been urging it in

The Budget-Hon. P. Martin this house for some time, as have other hon. members, as a means of providing some solution for the serious unemployment situation that attends the automobile industry. It is significant that Professor Bladen in making his recommendations, which are to be found on page 58 of his report-prepared, by the way, at a considerable expense and valuable only if it receives from the government the kind of attention it warrants-spoke of these proposals as a package, that one proposal by itself will not meet the purpose behind the commissioner's program. For instance, Professor Bladen says:
I want to emphasize, however, that these are not discrete items from which a selection is invited; they constitute a unitary plan, a program for the continued development of the automotive industry in Canada.
The government is not in any way implementing the comprehensive program put forward in the Bladen commission report. Thus far the government again gives evidence of procrastination, perhaps until a further crisis in the industry takes place. I say that we welcome, of course, the elimination of the 7J per cent excise tax, but I say that the government should have recognized this three years ago when it was faced with the large volume of unemployment that confronted the automobile industry. Automobiles are no longer luxuries. The mere recognition of the fact does not do justice to the difficulties being experienced by the industry.
There are a number of factors that must be looked upon in mitigation of the impact of the reduction of this tax provided for at so late a date. I say that I welcome the elimination of this tax, but if this action had been taken three years ago some of the things about which 1 am now going to speak would not exist.
First of all, the value of used cars is likely to decline in proportion to the reduction in the price of new cars, so that the majority of purchasers who wish to trade in cars will not realize a full 7J per cent reduction in price. Second, if the government is successful in its policy of devaluing the Canadian dollar, the cost of Canadian produced automobiles is bound to rise because of the large American parts content. The minister argued the converse, of course, last year when, in referring to the high premium on the Canadian dollar, he said as found on page 2673 of Hansard:
On the other hand, it lowers the cost of imported raw materials and semi-finished goods used by our manufacturers, and it has helped keep down our cost of living and cost of producing.
But that is not the position taken by the minister in the current budget. I further point out that the pending 3 per cent sales tax, which Mr. Frost argues is necessary because of the fiscal arrangements with the federal

government, will itself absorb half the benefits accruing from the elimination of the federal excise tax in the province of Ontario, which is the largest market for Canadian produced automobiles. I refer to the second recommendation of Professor Bladen, which will be found on page 58 of the report and reads as follows:
That the base for the application of sales tax on imported motor vehicles, under the Excise Tax Act, be changed from the duty paid value to the sale price to the retailer in Canada, and that section 29(1) be amended accordingly.
But no, we do not have any indication whatsoever from the government, notwithstanding these observations of the royal commissioner. Professor Bladen said:
I know of no other country that places domestic manufacturers at a disadvantage in meeting import competition. The United Kingdom levies its purchase tax on imported goods, as on all goods, on their wholesale value in the United Kingdom. The United States applies its excise tax on all automobiles on the price of the automobile in condition for delivery to the purchaser in the United States.
