It will not allow companies to ascertain what the selling price of their products will be and it will have, in my opinion, a very detrimental effect on stabilizing the exports of this country.
I was very interested the other day to hear the remarks of the Minister of Public Works. Over the years until now he has had some influence in stabilizing the economy of this country through the exceedingly heavy expenditures we have made in the mortgage field through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. As I understood the minister's statement, he said that income tax today is lower than it has been for years. It seems to me this is in contradiction of the Financial Post, which on page 8 has a table headed:
Background to the budget. Where the revenue comes from. Income tax bite getting bigger.
This table shows that personal income tax in 1939 was 11 per cent; in 1950 it was 28 per cent; in 1961, 34 per cent. With regard to corporation income tax, in 1939 it was 19 per cent; in 1950, 27 per cent; in 1961, 26 per cent. This does not indicate to me that it is getting easier on the pocketbook of the workers of this country. I think they have a continuing problem in trying to make ends meet. The problems of income tax are not getting less but are getting more, and will continue to get worse. The only way income tax can be reduced is to increase the allowances for those in the low income group, and this has not been done. As long as those


paying income tax have to carry those thousands and thousands of people who are unemployed it will not be very easy to arrive at a situation that will be more advantageous.
It seems surprising to me also that a minister of the crown, and in particular one in as important a position as the Minister of Public Works, should have risen and made the speech he did make the other day. I do not think this is a reflection on the people he mentioned, but it is a reflection on those he did not mention and the fact that many of them have had no interest and are not willing on behalf of the people they represent to express an opinion on this budget and a number of other things about which they could have spoken. I think it is unfair for the government or any member of the cabinet to stand up in this house and say that the opposition takes up too much time; because on a number of occasions we have seen speaker after speaker on the government side talk about things which were only being discussed in order to give the government time to bring in legislation which they were not capable of bringing in earlier. Even in the last few weeks of this session we are still not sure what all the legislation in this session of parliament is going to be. It is interesting to note that the suggestions made by the Prime Minister as to what it is going to be are not necessarily those of the leader of the house, and each one has an opportunity to introduce something of his own.
It has been said that this government is interested in pushing the idea of socialism versus private enterprise. I believe that anyone, including the Prime Minister, who is interested in this argument should read the Ottawa letter which appears in Saturday Night of July 8. It says:
We have neither socialism nor private enterprise and are not going to go whole hog for either one or the other. Now, it seems clear, Mr. Diefenbaker's "issue" seems to boil down to "private profit versus crown corporations".
It goes on to say:
The back benches of the government are packed with little men who literally hate the crown corporations and their top executives. These M.P.'s are not big-minded enough to believe in the neutrality of civil servants.
The article goes on:
Similarly, the little men hate Donald Gordon and his C.N.R. They loathe the C.B.C. They cannot understand why profit-making crown corporation Polymer is not turned over to private pockets. And they want money-saving Eldorado Aviation turned over to private operators.
The article argues that this is in complete contradiction with what the Senate unemployment committee came up with when it

issued a report which made the whole socialism versus private enterprise battle completely irrelevant. The article goes on to say: "The maintenance of an adequate rate of economic growth requires a continuing high level of capital investment, both private and public. Private capital investment must be supplemented and stimulated by an adequate rate of government investment in social capital."
It goes on to mention that this government have considered this and are not in complete agreement with those who believe otherwise, because they are going to add to the capital of the industrial development bank so that government assistance can be given to the little people of this country.
I am particularly interested at the time of this budget in two or three matters which appear to me to be of great interest. One of them is this matter of where the Conservatives stand in relation to labour. This is going to be an important matter this summer. It is going to be discussed without doubt on a number of platforms, and I think we should take a look now at what the program of the government is.
I should like to mention two or three things. This morning I asked a question as to the government's intentions concerning Canadian postal employees. The question was simply this; does the government not believe that those people who are granted statutory holidays should be paid extra in respect of those statutory holidays when they have to work? Is it not the intention of the government to pay those people double time for the work they do on those days which would normally be days off and which are classed as statutory holidays?
If we read the long reply given by the Postmaster General on June 27, as reported at page 7107, we find it boils down to the fact that this government does not believe that employees are entitled to time off or that they should be paid extra for working on statutory holidays. They obviously do not believe in the system of double time for holidays that are worked. I suggest they probably also are in a position where they abuse, and widely abuse, this business of sick leave. In the reply by the minister he referred to the fact that they could take their sick leave and use the sick leave pay as compensation for the day they worked, though the fact that they did come in early every morning could be considered as overtime.
It is generally agreed by everybody who has thought about this matter at all that the interests of this country can only be served by bettering our labour code so that our workers may be in a continually better position to serve the needs of this country. I think it is a step in the wrong direction when the Canadian government itself gives no
The Budget-Mr. Peters assistance in the relationship it has with the postal employees in connection with this latest dispute.
This is shown in other ways. The Prime Minister himself said this year that the workers of the country, particularly those employed in the railway industry, would have an opportunity of presenting their case before a committee of this house. But when the matter of the railway workers was referred to that committee it did not concern all the railway workers of this country but only some of them, those employed by the Canadian National Railways. I believe there is a problem, well known to many members of this house, in relation to those C.P.R. workers who were pensioned off many years ago.
I refer to one example. An engineer who retired in 1953 and one who retired recently, both with 48 years' service, are treated in entirely different ways. The first receives a pension of $123.45 per month with no survivor benefit. The other receives a pension of $346.74. Should he predecease his wife she will receive a pension of $173.37. Her pension will be $49.92 higher than that of the first employee with 48 years of actual service as an engineer. Had the first engineer made provision for his wife his pension would have been reduced to less than $93 to provide her with a pension of less than $46. There were nearly 900 pensioners in British Columbia in 1953 receiving pensions of less than $51 per month with no survivor benefit, who were, at that time, given no consideration whatever.
This same condition applies at every terminal on the Canadian Pacific Railway from coast to coast. All pensioned employees for whom we speak, had they been employed by the Canadian National Railways, would have received equal treatment on the basis of service and income with those who were retired after January 1, 1953, including a survivor benefit.
We raise these matters because they indicate that this government is not being honest with the Canadian people when it says it wants to speak for labour and give labour a fair deal. We should look at what this pension plan really amounts to. It could, of course, be argued that the Canadian National is a government owned railway while the Canadian Pacific is not. I do not pretend to discuss now the merits of the Canadian National as against the Canadian Pacific, but it is simply not true that the Canadian Pacific has stood on its own two feet. I think it could be argued over the years we have spent almost as much on the C.P.R. as we have on the C.N.R. I would not even go so far as to say that we owe much more to one than

The Budget-Mr. Peters we do to the other. I do suggest, however, that these pensioners have not been given any consideration during all these years. The position of that company was not such as to warrant the statement that they could not afford to pay increases to these people on pension.
In looking at the annual report of the Canadian Pacific Railway for 1952, we find that the total reserves and unadjusted credits amount to $555,843,167, which is a sizeable sum of money. By 1960, deferred credits, reserves and provision for depreciation totalled $1,057,665,415. This would indicate to me that we have given a great deal of money, through subsidies and other means to this company in return for which we have received very little, especially by way of consideration for employees who have been helpful during all these years in establishing and maintaining that company.
I believe, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister was less than fair when he referred to a committee this matter of Canadian National pensions and did not include the question of Canadian Pacific pensions. It seems to me that all these people who believe in the free enterprise system, the social credit members and the union nationale members, are not willing to refer the question of Canadian Pacific Railway operations to a committee, and thus prove to the members of the house that this company is all that is alleged to be. I am suggesting that these members of the house should be willing to follow this course if they are going to be fair to labour and to the Conservative party.
The unemployment insurance fund has been practically depleted. The government has suggested that they are going to put in $170 million to tide this fund over a difficult period. This step should have been taken a long time ago. The fund should never have been allowed to get into the depleted condition in which it is now. I believe that this amount should have been added to the fund, and more, rather than using it as a subsidy to finance government operations in dealing with the recession, something for which this government was responsible.
In recent days, Mr. Speaker, this government has done something else to which labour will have to give some consideration. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) asked a question the other day concerning lay-offs at the Saskatoon plant of Westeel Products Limited. Evidently the unemployment insurance commission office there had suspended these employees from receiving benefits because of a rumour to the effect the employees had been laid off in anticipation of a strike. Does this action not mean

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget debate as well as the speech of the minister and the budget itself which we are now considering have inevitably prompted the question in our minds: Why has "expansionist" finance become a government slogan after four years of recession and slow-down during which the government rejected proposals for expansionist finance from this side whenever they were put forward? Well, the question perhaps is not too difficult to answer. The answer is that we are approaching an election.
This budget has been described by the minister as an economic budget. Well, it is an economic budget in the sense perhaps that it is not itself an election budget; the

The Budget-Mr. Pearson glamorous political gifts are to come next time. The good features in this budget-and there are some, we put some of them forward ourselves-are four years late, but the weaknesses and inadequacy of the budget, and I hope to point out some of the weaknesses, will be felt now.
This budget is a confession of the failure of the government to do anything really effective during four years to halt the decline in our development; a decline shown by the fact-and this cannot be disputed in this house or outside of it-that real output per capita has decreased in those four years, while in the previous eight years it had increased by 20 per cent. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this budget is simply further evidence that we have a government which mistakes words for action, which is more concerned with the sensation created than the result achieved. It seems to think that cleverness in politics is a substitute for skill, wisdom and steadiness in government, and that excitement is a substitute for efficiency.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He says production had increased 20 per cent. Will he indicate how much of that was price increase?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A substantial portion; I could not indicate the figures. I do not know what the price increase was in the eight years; perhaps the hon. member knows more accurately than I do. It would be something like 4 per cent, or 5 per cent, if I had to hazard a guess, but I am not sure.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I put on the record this morning, if I remember rightly, that from 1945 to 1952 it was 50 per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, even if it was 50 per cent-I am not accepting these figures, I just do not know; my hon. friend has not put them forward as being accurate, but even if that were the case-it would still leave a real increase per capita of 10 per cent against an actual decrease in the four years. However, the attitude of the government, the effectiveness of the government is shown, as I was beginning to point out, by the fact, in our view, that problems are allowed to drag on until they become crises. We have said this many times over here. Then expedients are frantically sought out too late, however, to deal with those crises, while a smokescreen is thrown up to conceal failure to act in time. I could give many examples to support that statement. For instance, unemployment was not even, in the eyes of the government, a really serious problem until the autumn of 1960.


The railway problem was allowed to drag on until it became critical, when a subsidy was thrown in, as usual, as a stopgap. Defence policy is in a state of confused indecision. We are spending millions and millions on we know not what kind of defence.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You don't know but everybody else knows.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We do know one thing, Mr. Speaker, namely that we are buying a secondhand United States interceptor to replace a first class Canadian plane that was scrapped and sunk without a trace except the trace of bitter resentment and national chagrin.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The most impractical effort any government ever made was to start that plane.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Monetary policy is no responsibility of the government. That is the position they took up till February last. When Mr. Coyne exposed the fallacy and, indeed, the danger of that attitude, four years later a royal commission is set up to deal with the problem. We have advocated formally by resolution in this house that monetary policy should be a subject for parliamentary inquiry and investigation, and this should have been done a long time ago. International trade problems can be evaded while the government preaches and lectures and waits for something to happen in Europe. A budget should be balanced, until five failures to do so convert a deficit into a suddenly discovered virtue. And so on and so on and so on- confusion, indecision and delay.
These are the methods that were followed in the production of the budget which we are now considering. It was produced after unprecedented delay and unprecedented excitement, disturbance and crisis for which the government is responsible and which culminated in the unhappy controversy over the governor of the Bank of Canada. The impression was created by all this excitement, and perhaps it was meant to be created, that something really important, something really big, was to be included in the budget, something to lead us out of the valley of recession again, into the uplands of expansion, growth and prosperity, something that would constitute a massive attack on unemployment which remains so distressingly high, higher indeed than the same time last year in spite of all the complacent predictions of ministers.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, this budget was to have been such an intoxicating one that the governor of the Bank of Canada was to be forced to resign before he could see it. As it happened, there is not very much in the budget to cause him any surprise or provoke much disagreement with it or to give adequate

stimulus to our economy which needs that stimulus so badly. In short, the budget did not live up to its advance billing.
Indeed, so little of expansion is there in the inadequate measures of this budget that the minister himself predicts an increase in our gross national product for the current year of only 3 per cent. That is less than last year when the gross national product was not enough to produce jobs in mid-winter for more than three quarters of a million people. We can perhaps take some comfort from the fact that the minister may be as far off in this prediction as in the others he has made.
This year is to be another deficit year but it is not an expansion deficit. The nature of the budget makes that clear in spite of all the words of the minister in his attempt to prove the contrary. Away back in June, 1958, the Minister of Finance had this to say. I think I have quoted these words already but they bear repetition.
These huge deficits ... carry serious implications for the ... future health ... of our country.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we have had four more since then, accidental and unplanned. The minister chided us and me in particular last evening with inconsistency but what did he say just a year ago? I quote from his budget speech of that time:
The restoration of a balanced budget this year-
That was 1960.
-constitutes the achievement of an objective to which we have been moving purposefully and deliberately for some time. The position we have now reached, with its solid prospect of a fully balanced budget, represents the fruits of carefully designed policies; it is not something that just happened.
That is quite true. It did not happen. The minister's predictions last year were as wrong as his recent praise of a deficit rings hollow. It is true that the minister as a prophet on economic matters still thunders in the best old testament style but few of his prophecies are being fulfilled. So we have learned from experience to take him with several grains of salt when he starts forecasting. Perhaps he will be as bad a prophet this year as in the others. After all, last year he predicted a $12 million surplus which became a $345 million deficit. The reason he gives for that mistake in the white paper is that unfortunately 1960 was a year not of the solid expansion predicted but of adjustment and of special complexity. Indeed, on page 46 of the white paper he finally breaks down and admits that the economy has slowed down since this government took office.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Doom and gloom.
The Budget-Mr. Pearson

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: So his record of predictions is not a very respectable one. In his budget speech in 1960 the minister made other predictions which in the light of experience have been shown to be away out. We all remember that he said that the gross national product would go up 6 per cent. In fact, we got an increase of 3.2 per cent and only 2 per cent in constant dollars. Yet when I commented in the house on the minister's predictions in my budget speech last year and said that this and certain other predictions were too optimistic, when I said that in my view the increase in the gross national product would more likely be 3.5 per cent-I was a little optimistic-and that there would be serious difficulties in 1960 with regard to unemployment, and when I asked the minister at that time what plans the government had to meet these economic difficulties which we felt were looming up the minister again wrapped the flag around himself and accused us of impugning the honour and reputation of Canada and of selling our country short. Unhappily, Mr. Speaker, we were right and he was wrong.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Again.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister and his colleagues are no scoundrels but patriotism is often their last refuge against argument that cannot be met in any other way. Look at unemployment. The minister said last year that the situation would improve. In fact we know now that the average during 1960 was 7 per cent compared with 6 per cent in 1959. Capital expenditures in 1960 were $8,200 million or 2.6 per cent below 1959. Capital expenditures in this country as a percentage of gross national production were 22.8 per cent, which is the lowest since 1951.
An increase in private investment was forecast by the minister's colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees), in one of his predictions. He said it would increase 4 per cent whereas in fact it decreased 2.6 per cent. So, Mr. Speaker, how can we have confidence in this government's fiscal policies and in their administration of them when the Minister of Finance can be so wrong in his assessment of economic conditions in this country and of the government's financial accounts?
Even the minister himself no longer has that same buoyant confidence in his predictions of things to come.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you sure?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This year he refused to give us a straightforward and clear-cut forecast for the increase in the gross national product in 1961. He is becoming a little more careful
7258	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Pearson as he goes on because this is what he said as found on page 6640 of Hansard:
But this improvement-
He is talking about the expected improvement which we all hope will take place:
-which could be expected in the ordinary course of events and without further stimulus, would, I believe, be modest, an increase of about 3 per cent in the G.N.P.
This is less than last year. So the minister has become, in my opinion, overcautious and that is quite a change. In 1960 which was a recession year, the increase was 3.2 per cent. In 1961, a year in which the Prime Minister and the other ministers tell us that the recession is over, the Minister of Finance predicts a rise of only 3 per cent, less than last year. The minister has become a prophet of doom and gloom.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We need at least 6 per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In a year in which he says the recession is over, he only has the confidence to predict an increase in the G.N.P. which is less than last year, a year of recession. How is he going to explain that? He has been telling us that the recession is lifting. If it is lifting we shall surely have in our production next year a greater increase than 3 per cent, which was not enough last year to prevent massive unemployment and slow down.
Why has the minister become so pessimistic and so cautious in his forecasting? I can see one reason and I have a feeling that it is the right reason. The minister wants to be in a position to tell us next year that the actual increase has exceeded his expectations. I can picture him in the house, if he is here then, saying that his expectations were exceeded and that the outcome could be due only to his budget and government policies. The modesty of the minister this year is merely intended to serve as a background for his glorification next year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Having been struck out four times.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Next year he may feel will be the year before the election. I am prepared to say this, and although he does not need it I should be glad to give the minister permission now to quote these words a year hence if we are both here. I am prepared to say that the minister will be wrong again this year, but for once and for the only time since he has been minister he will be wrong on the conservative side.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is hedging now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In spite of the government's lack of effective policies and because of the hard work of our people, because of price increases-and I shall have something to say about their probability later-because of the resilience of our economy and because of business improvement across the line, I believe that the gross national product in current dollars will be higher than that estimated by the minister.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is statesmanship for you; not politics.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am also prepared to say that the average level of unemployment in 1961, in spite of the minister's claim will be at least as high as that in 1960 and in spite of the minister's claim that there is nothing structurally wrong with our economy. The minister has been converted in another respect.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Somersaults.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is making a good many trips to the penitent's bench these days.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He should do so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We all remember how he used to lecture us in this house and how Mr. Coyne used to lecture us also in the country in sombre terms about the dangers of uncontrolled expansion and inflation, and this at a time when we were in the midst of a recession with massive unemployment. Now that we are told that we are out of the recession and that we are on the road to full recovery and expansion again, as the Prime Minister keeps on assuring us, in this situation, which should result in an increase of inflationary pressure, the minister now tells us that any serious danger of inflation has disappeared. I had better quote him. I think these words have already been put on the record. As found at page 6649 of Hansard he said this:
I do not think that we are in any serious danger of inflation under present circumstances, with so much unused capacity in our economy. A decline in the exchange rate will mean modest price advances for some of the goods we obtain from abroad as well as some of our export commodities. I am confident, however, that if under present conditions of unused economic capacity there is any effect on consumer prices and the cost of living-
And he used these words again last night.
-these will be minimal.
I suppose that means practically not noticeable. I believe that when the minister presents his next annual budget, he will have to admit that he has been wrong here, that prices will start to rise again-indeed they are starting already-and that inflation will

be, in the present circumstances, a real danger, as it was in the booming mid fifties. But the great difference with that earlier period will be that the rise in prices now will be largely due to government policies and will be accompanied by unused capacity and abnormal unemployment, whereas in that earlier period it was caused by shortages and bottlenecks in the private sector of our economy. Last year the minister overestimated the rise in the G.N.P. and the danger of inflation. This year I think he has underestimated both.
There is an even more spectacular conversion of the minister. This is his conversion to the virtues of deficit financing.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A planned deficit.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The threat of yesterday has become the opportunity of today. The economic threat of yesterday has become the political opportunity of today. Listen to this excerpt from his budget speech, from this always flexible but now expanding minister. As found at page 6642 of Hansard he said this:
When there is a substantial degree of slackness in the economy .. . budget deficits can provide an important stimulus... If appropriately planned and timed-
Then he says: in present circumstances a sizeable deficit will help to stimulate the economy.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A year too late.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why did the minister not talk like this and act on this talk in those earlier years when a deficit in an emergency situation for stimulating the economy and planned for that purpose would have been of such great value.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He did not see it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister now says that if we quarrel with his conversion to deficit financing we are contradicting ourselves. He went to some lengths to prove this or in attempting to prove this last evening. Our position on this matter has not changed. No one likes going into debt, or he should not like going into debt either personally or nationally. However, when you are in trouble, borrowing can be essential to get you out of trouble but only for that purpose. If it achieves that purpose, then you stop borrowing and begin to put something by, if you are wise, for the next rainy day. But the minister now says we are out of trouble or soon will be out of trouble but we are going to borrow more than ever. The minister in this respect is not contradicting others as he accused me of doing last night. He is contradicting himself, something which is worse.
May I now say a few words about the budget itself, and about the policies that are
The Budget-Mr. Pearson put forward in the budget. The budget contains several policy announcements but, of course, it is also remarkable for its omissions. There is nothing in the budget for agriculture. Does that mean that the wheat producers will not even get this year the $1 per acre payment they received last year, the virtues of which the Prime Minister was preaching yesterday on the prairies? Does this mean, also, that the government claims that eastern farmers have no problems and do not have to face serious difficulties, at a time when their income continues to decline?
There is nothing in the budget to assist the long range development and short range unemployment difficulties of the Atlantic provinces. Surely the government must now realize that its provision for double depreciation is completely inadequate and in its application much too restrictive, if I may use that word, to do the job. If we want to remove the hardship of unemployment and stagnation; if we want our economy to get moving again, we must begin by effective means of assistance-if I may use the expression without being misunderstood-for our economically depressed areas. So far as the opposition are concerned, we have insisted since 1958 on the urgent necessity of remedying this situation of regional chronic unemployment.
In March, 1961, for instance, I put forward in this house a six point program of regional recovery. We had a two day debate on this important matter at that time. But the government, in spite of the most solemn promises which it made in 1958, has refused to do anything adequate for the development of the Atlantic provinces or other underdeveloped areas in this country.
What about trade policy? The Minister of Finance told us a few days before the budget -and somewhat surprisingly because of his record-that he was in favour of an expansionist trade policy. He devoted quite a long section of his budget speech to trade matters, but it was the old lecture. Canada, he said, would continue to adhere to GATT and to respect her international obligations. He suggested at least, if he did not say so in precise terms, that those of us on this side who were advocating proposals looking for an Atlantic free trade area which would be open to any country in the world to enter on the terms which were applicable to the others, were advocating a kind of restrictionist bilateral approach to trade problems. Not at all. This is the way to approach multilateral trade in the present circumstances.
The minister then said this. This is the only indication of his understanding this particular problem:

The Budget-Mr. Pearson
We shall, of course, have to adapt to changes in the world around us and be alert and flexible in meeting new challenges and opportunities as they arise. For the present at least the situation is much too unsettled to consider seriously a sharp reorientation in our policies along these lines.
In other words, let us wait and see. Let us change our policy, if necessary, only after other countries change theirs and when it may be too late to safeguard, let alone promote, our own interests. What a revealing Conservative attitude:	We will not promote
necessary change but we will adapt to the changes which are being made by others which are forced upon us. In this connection I would draw attention to Europe. Where is the positive, dynamic and imaginative trade policy that our country so urgently and so badly needs at this time?
I now come, Mr. Speaker, to the budget proposals which will, according to the minister, transform our recent toils and trials to new triumphs. They can be divided into four main categories. I shall say only a few words about each. There is the exchange rate policy, debt management and interest rates policies, fiscal policy including tax changes, and the deficit.
First the exchange rate policy, about which there has been a good deal said by hon. members on this side of the house. I do not think we need apologize for that because this is certainly one of the most important features of the budget. The minister has at last come to the conclusion that the high premium on the Canadian dollar was hurting our economy. He is now prepared, with all the risks involved-some of which were pointed out by my hon. friend from Essex East this afternoon-to see the exchange fund used to bring down the exchange rate of our dollar. The words he used-and these are the words which cause us so much uneasiness- were to bring the dollar down "to a significant discount".
On this side of the house we have been deploring the high premium on the Canadian dollar since the recession of 1957-58 and we have been steadily advocating appropriate remedial government policies. Notwithstanding what the minister tried to say last evening in accusing us of contradicting ourselves, we still support that view. But the minister has certainly drastically changed his view. Last year-and I think these words were quoted this afternoon-he deplored the high premium, but he claimed that it resulted from "the free play of forces of supply and demand", and he strongly opposed an arbitrary and artificial attempt by the government to work against basic economic forces.
Well, what is he doing now? He had this to say, as reported at page 2673 of Hansard:

An attempt by the government artificially to lower the external price of the Canadian dollar would involve borrowing or raising by taxes very large sums of money with which to buy up foreign exchange.
Then a little later:
In other words we would be embarking upon a gigantic financial speculation with no assurance of success.
Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what the minister is doing now. He is proposing to do just that, to use the exchange fund in "an arbitrary and artificial attempt by the government" to bring about a "significant discount". This was a late conversion by the minister, but we are always glad to see him make progress in understanding and wisdom. But we disagree with the uncertainty of his goal and the danger of speculation which will be created by that uncertainty. We disagree, as has already been pointed out on this side of the house, with the methods he proposes to use in order to reach that goal, if indeed it is a goal at all.
By refusing to define what he means by a "significant discount", the minister will certainly create uncertainty and confusion, if he has not already done so, which surely can only adversely affect our external financial transactions. What is a significant discount- 3 per cent, 5 per cent, 10 per cent, or more? Nobody knows. What a wonderful opportunity for gambling.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The worst kind of speculation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister wants to control the price of our dollar arbitrarily but he does not know where he wants it to be. He will not disclose the discount he wishes to achieve. What could be more arbitrary and artificial than that approach? The significant discount could be 3 per cent one week and I suppose it could be 5 per cent the following week, these figures to be maintained not by market action but presumably by governmental action. How can our exporters and importers carry on their business on that basis, with the constant threat of governmental interference with market forces but with no fixed objective to be attained by that intervention? Surely that is another example of wrong and arbitrary use of ministerial authority.
The elimination of the premium on the Canadian dollar is certainly a worth-while objective. We have been saying that on this side of the house for a long time. It should have been sought long ago. Our trading partners and competitors would then have undoubtedly understood our position and accepted such a move. But to seek to achieve a significant but undetermined discount now through arbitrary governmental action of the

nature proposed by the minister, when we have no currency difficulties, is something very different indeed.
The government is trying to secure through exchange fund operations advantages and benefits which it was not able to secure through tariff and trade negotiations. We are also, presumably, going to try through this kind of action to give greater protection to our domestic industries because we are unable directly to increase tariffs generally due to our international obligations under GATT. The minister has pointed out that we must remain true to them, and I agree. What would happen to international trade and ordinary financial transactions in the world if all other nations were doing what our government is now proposing to do? In so doing, the minister certainly violates the spirit of GATT although in another part of his speech he proclaimed that Canada-and I have quoted this already-must remain a law abiding member of the international financial and commercial community.
What about our position in relation to the international monetary fund? Surely this must be giving the minister some cause for worry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, the hon. gentleman should be worrying about it. While other nations have a fixed exchange rate which they cannot change without the approval of the fund, Canada has been able to avoid this rigidity because we have been willing to let market forces determine our floating exchange rate. What will happen now? Can we be the only member of the fund which can devalue its currency through government action without having an obligation to seek the approval of the other members of the fund? Why should Canada be placed in this preferred position? Perhaps the minister would explain that. It must also be pointed out that this significant devaluation of the Canadian dollar will have certain adverse effects. It will have certain advantageous effects, too, of course, in so far as it will benefit our exporters. If it does that, and the benefits are maintained, that is all to the good. But it will impose-and the minister will surely not deny this-an additional financial burden on the provinces and municipalities which in recent years have been forced to borrow on the American market because of tight money conditions and the high interest rates prevailing in our own economy. Moreover, producers and consumers will also suffer to the extent that they rely on imported goods the prices of which, if they are imported from the United States, will go up.
When the minister last year referred to the high premium on the Canadian dollar he had
The Budget-Mr. Pearson this to say, and I think these words were quoted by my hon. friend from Essex East:
On the other hand it-
That is, lowering the premium on the dollar.
-lowers the cost of imported raw materials and semi-finished goods used by manufacturers. It has helped to keep down our cost of living and the cost of producing.
It has helped, he said, to keep down our cost of living. The minister now reverses that policy. Does he deny, then, that one effect of this reversal might be to help to increase the cost of living?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Conditions are different now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is true. I have just said that. Conditions are different in the sense that we are told-and I hope it is right-that we are getting out of the recession. If we are getting out of the recession then our productive capacity is being more and more used and in these circumstances inflationary pressures will be stronger and this kind of exchange action should have a greater effect on the cost of living than it would have had if it had been taken earlier.
The minister has deplored the high level of capital inflow in recent years. He deplored -and I can understand his anxiety because it is one we all share-foreign control and particularly United States control over our industries. He referred to this in his budget speech as reported at page 6645 of Hansard. But that process of foreign capital moving into this country and investing in and taking over our industries will be easier by reason of this exchange action. A significant devaluation of the Canadian dollar will inevitably depreciate the value of Canadian assets in terms of the American dollar and it will give an additional inducement and an additional advantage to American investors as opposed to Canadian investors to purchase existing Canadian firms and do the very thing the minister says he is trying to prevent.
Now we come to debt management and interest rates. The minister, who is the very model of inconsistency, had this to say about interest rates on February 21, 1961. That is not very long ago. He said:
Lest the impression be created in the minds of some hon. members that the government has brought about high interest rates let me point out that interest rates in this country, while they are higher than the government would like to see on borrowings it has to make are lower than the interest rates in the United Kingdom and have been close to the 1960 rates of interest in the United States, the country which is the largest reservoir of capital in the world and whose rates traditionally are lower than interest rates in Canada.

The Budget-Mr. Pearson
That statement appears at page 2267 of Hansard. What does the minister say now? What did he say the other evening in this house as reported at page 6645?
-interest rates in Canada are out of line with those in the United States and some of the European capital exporting countries. We should like to see these spreads narrowed.
Well, I am not aware and I doubt if the minister is aware that those spreads have widened since February.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, they have.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At that time, according to the minister, they did not exist or they were normal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They have widened since.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In any case, the minister is telling us that he is now in favour of lowering interest rates, another conversion that comes a little late. The lowering of interest rates and easier credit should have been initiated long before now. But the minister in those days said he was fighting inflation. That, according to him, was the primary danger and his sermon was based on the theme of work and save, down with the demon of inflation. He wanted expansion, of course. We all wanted expansion. But he was worried about the kind of expansion we might get and its effect on inflation. Well, the minister in his budget now is giving to the government a set of conflicting policy objectives. I think it is easy to demonstrate this.
What about the demand for funds? This, in the months, ahead, would certainly have an effect on interest rates. If, as we are continually being told, the Canadian economy is on the road to recovery, private demands for loans will inevitably increase. Moreover, all the provinces and a great number of municipalities have already announced that they are planning for cash deficits in 1961 and 1962 and their demands for funds or their borrowing requirements will undoubtedly be heavy. Finally, according to the minister's own estimates, the new borrowing requirements of the federal government are likely to exceed $1 billion, a fact which now gives the hon. gentleman more comfort than the concern it used to give him if we can interpret his remarks last night. This means, surely, that the demand for funds is likely to increase rapidly in this country during the latter part of the current fiscal year. The decision announced by the minister with respect to debt management-and he put forward these figures as a mitigating force which will neutralize, perhaps, in his mind, this danger-will not do very much to curb this demand, or to reduce the pressures which are 
likely to be exerted on our financial markets. The intention, and I use the words of the minister, "to confine new federal market issues for at least the next several months to the 'short end' of the market", is supposed to be one of the things that will save us. That, of course, is not new. Since the great conversion loan most of the borrowings of the federal government have been, I believe, of a short term nature. The change to be made in the portfolio of the unemployment insurance fund is not likely to have any material effect at a time when, we are told and we hope, disbursements will now begin to be in better balance with the revenue of the fund. That is the only possible explanation one can give to the government's refusal to do anything about the fund. Finally, there is the establishment of a purchase fund of $100 million-I do not know where that is coming from-for the orderly retirement of government debt. This cannot possibly have any material influence on the market during the current fiscal year.
So much for demands. Now, what about the supply of funds to meet these rapidly increasing demands and the effect this will have on the minister's policy of trying to get interest rates down. The three main sources of supply are the savings of the Canadian people, the net capital inflow from abroad and changes in the money supply. The minister admitted the other night that the rate of Canadian savings is-I have not got his exact words-already high and reasonably satisfactory and this source of supply is not likely to increase very much with a mild recovery. In any event, he did not hold out any exaggerated-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did not say the
latter part of that sentence.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, I will adopt the latter part as my own words, that supply from this source is not likely to increase very much with a mild recovery.
The second source is capital inflow. The government wants a lower level of capital inflow and has already taken steps to bring that about. Finally, the minister has ruled out, and rightly so, the possibility of a rapid increase in the money supply. I hope that in the face of all the pressure which will begin to develop he will stick to this. The minister said, as reported at page 6645 of Hansard:
It would be folly, for example, to attempt drastically and artificially to force interest rates down by irresponsible increases in the money supply. Such a device would be not only unsound but before long would prove to be self-defeating.
He is certainly right in that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would you mind reading the next sentence?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would be delighted to read the next sentence, but I have not got it here. Perhaps if I am unfair to the minister he would give me the next sentence, because I am sure he would remember it.
Under such conditions of supply and demand we would expect higher, not lower, interest rates and tight, not easier, money. Yet the minister says that he wants-and I have no doubt he does want-to reduce interest rates and to bring about improvements in our capital markets which will be of direct benefit to the provinces, municipalities, business and other borrowers. That was, he claims, one of the main reasons why he found it necessary to get rid of the governor of the Bank of Canada. It will be interesting to see how the minister will achieve all these conflicting objectives he has now indicated. I predict that if economic conditions develop as he has indicated, and if he respects all his other commitments, as he will no doubt desire to do, he will not be able to reduce interest rates or to maintain the money supply at a responsible level as he promised.
We come now to fiscal policies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I can give the Leader of the Opposition the page now; the second column of page 6645, beginning with the words, "We attach".

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think I had better read it because I do not believe the minister should be quoted in part.
We attach high importance to a climate of confidence and understanding in our financial markets. What is required is a judicious and well coordinated combination of fiscal, monetary and general economic measures, the elements of which vary in acordance with the needs of the times.
That is an admirable doctrine. I am certainly glad to repeat that because the minister emphasizes the desirability and necessity of co-ordinating fiscal and monetary policy. It was not very long ago that the minister was saying he had no responsibility for monetary policy. He now says that in an effort to reduce interest rates and get easier money it is absolutely vital that there is a co-ordination of fiscal, economic and monetary policies. This co-ordination can now be brought about by a government which refused to take responsibility for monetary policy.
I come to fiscal policy and, in particular, to the tax changes which normally would constitute the proof of the minister's claim that this is indeed an expansionist budget. The tax reductions, as we have so often been told in this debate, in the current year will amount
The Budget-Mr. Pearson to $65 million. Of this $65 million, $55 million will come from the elimination of the excise tax on automobiles. I am not going to deal with that because the hon. member for Essex East, who is primarily responsible for the removal of this excise tax, has dealt with it in some detail and pointed out that the benefits which it is hoped will come from the removal of the tax will be modified by certain circumstances which have arisen, including the sales tax in Ontario, the reduction of the exchange rate which will increase the value of imports and the reduction of the allowance for secondhand cars.
However, taking that $55 million out of the $65 million of tax reduction, what have we left? We have $10 million in tax reductions. Surely, we are not going to get a miracle of expansion from this. If that is the measure of the so-called expansionist fiscal policies of the minister, he certainly misled the Canadian people when he made his statement in the house on June 14 about a budget which was meant to be so sensational but which was, in fact, such an anti-climax. We on this side have recommended on more than one occasion during recent years that tax incentives, including specific tax exemptions and reductions, be used to promote a healthy economic development in our country, particularly in a time of recession when the economy has to get a shot in the arm for expansion purposes. The objectives sought by the minister in proposing tax changes in this budget affecting business are sound and sensible, although again they are too late in terms of our economic condition.
However, the methods which he puts forward, as is so often the case when his principles are sound, are completely inadequate and ineffective. Let us consider the technique of accelerated depreciation about which he has made so much. When applied within the limit of capital cost allowances not exceeding 100 per cent, this measure can at best be useful as an anti-recession measure only in persuading business to accelerate its investment program but it cannot induce industry to increase and enlarge such programs. The reason, of course, is that accelerated depreciation, applied within the limited context of 100 per cent capital cost allowance, merely means a deferred tax payment. This is precisely what is wrong with the minister's tax proposal. He wants to use a device which can induce business to re-schedule its investment plan in the short run, and that may be desirable, to promote long term industrial development and to stimulate economic expansion. In spite of the minister's claims for this proposal, the only objective conclusion to be drawn is

The Budget-Mr. Pearson that the proposed tax changes will have very little effect indeed on the rate of growth of Canada's economy.
We are, therefore, left with a deficit as the real shot in the arm for the economy, a deficit which includes $65 million of tax reduction of which $55 million comes from the removal of the excise tax on automobiles. The minister has told us that he does not know what this deficit is going to be. It might be $600 million, it might be $650 million or it might be $700 million. He sort of hit a medium amount between $600 million and $700 million and suggested it may be $650 million. One thing is sure. According to the minister his deficit was planned. He repeated last night that it is a planned deficit this time, and it is timely. It has come just at the right time.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Everything at the right time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, the deficit of course was not planned at all. The best evidence of this is that it was forecast months ago by the Canadian tax foundation. Were they planning the deficit for the minister? There is no more planning for expansionist purposes in this deficit than there was for last year's deficit which began as a surplus and ended as a deficit of $345 million. It might not have been quite so high if it had not been for Good Friday.
Surely the minister cannot contend that this was a planned deficit. On top of the deficit, the estimates prepared in the fall of 1960 involved an increase of $383 million as compared with the main estimates of 1960-61. According to the minister when he tabled those estimates on January 26, I think it was, of last year, what accounted for this increase? The minister at that time indicated- and I think he had something to say about this last night-that the two main factors accounting for the increase in the estimates were civil service salaries and conditional payments to the provinces, especially to Quebec for the hospitalization plan. As we see it, Mr. Speaker, such increased expenditures could hardly have been planned to meet the economic conditions. Assuming no increase in revenues in 1961-62, as compared with 196061, rising expenditures added to the deficit of $345 million last year would have produced in the current year a deficit of $728 million, which is very close to the estimate given by the minister.
So much for planning. On the revenue side the minister expects an increase in 1961-62 of only $150 million. While he announced tax reductions valued at $65 million it remains true to say that the lack of growth in revenue is mainly due to the recent recession and to the current stagnation. On the basis

of this evidence, it is clear that the minister shows no respect for himself or for the facts when he claims that he planned the deficit this year to bring about expansion.
We also claim, contrary to what the minister has said, that this deficit is badly timed as well as being not expansionist. We are told by the minister, we are told by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Trade and Commerce ad nauseam, that 1961 will be a year of recovery. We hope it will be. In terms of cyclical pattern, therefore, this year should be compared with 1959 as a year of recovery, while 1958 should be compared with 1960 as a low point in the recession. I think the minister will agree with that. What do we get now in terms of government policies in a year of cyclical recovery but when our structural and long term problems are becoming more evident? In spite of the evidence of recovery we get not an expansion but an antirecession program, with a record, unplanned, peacetime deficit brought about by increased fixed expenditures, which will create inflationary pressures but with no effective measures to deal with the long term structural problems and above all our chronic unemployment. This is why we claim this budget is ineffective and inadequate.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I will sum up our criticism of government economic policies as expressed in this budget and in the minister's statement.
First, we believe that those economic policies are ill-timed, confused and inconsistent.
Second, we believe that the measures proposed by the minister to bring about an uncertain but a "significant" depreciation of the Canadian dollar are not likely to achieve the results that are hoped for and are fraught with danger.
Third, in the field of monetary and debt management policy, the government will have to choose between lower interest rates and a sound increase in the money supply. It will not be able to achieve those two objectives at the same time, especially if it succeeds in reducing foreign capital inflow.
Fourth, the tax incentives provided in the budget will not succeed in bringing the balanced long term growth which is now essential.
Fifth, the government's fiscal policy, as outlined, is not suited for a period of recovery on which it is based and it is not designed to meet the structural problems of the Canadian economy.
Sixth, the fiscal deal with the provinces greatly weakens the principle of equalization and will result in growing regional inequalities which are bound to weaken our federal system.

Seventh, the budget provides no special development assistance to the Atlantic provinces and other areas of underdevelopment and over unemployment.
Finally, in the field of trade policy, the government maintains its creeping protectionism but refuses to face the challenge created by the emergence of new and important trading blocs in the world. In other words, this budget contains a few good measures but they are too little and too late, and they are not capable of dealing with the problem in this country as it should be dealt with at this time.
Many people in this country now agree that this government-and how right they are-is drifting, confused and inconsistent; that in four years this Conservative government has created a financial mess without succeeding in solving the serious difficulties experienced by the economy during those four years, the most important evidence of which is the continuance of massive unemployment. All the facts are there and the minister cannot deny them. He cannot deny them through official records.
Since 1957 our gross public debt will have increased by $4.3 billion and our net debt by more than $2 billion; and yet the volume of our gross national product per capita has declined by 5 per cent, and this is an official figure. Unemployment has reached record levels exceeded only during the great depression of the 1930's and agriculture is still facing serious difficulties. These facts are becoming more and more known to the Canadian people in spite of the huge and continuous outflow of Conservative propaganda. Of course, Mr. Speaker, there is no easy way out of the mess which has been created over a period of more than four years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If there is a mess it goes back a good deal more than four years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Whenever we talk about the past four years my hon. friend likes to talk about the years previous to those four years. How many people in Canada would love to go back to those years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do you want to find out?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We do indeed want to find out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How soon?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I ask the minister to do his best to influence the Prime Minister to give us the opportunity as soon as possible. Mr. Speaker, more and more people are looking back to those days of steady and businesslike
The Budget-Mr. R. A. Bell management of our affairs, days of full employment, days of exciting national development, days of great national progress, days when Canada had a great influence in the councils of the world. Our main criticism of this budget, Mr. Speaker, is that it does nothing to give us any hope that those days will be restored.

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard A. Bell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in incredulous fascination has the house listened this afternoon in the course of the debate to the speech of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and that of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). The big guns of Liberalism have been mustered in a final assault on this budget. Really, sir, I should have said the obsolete big guns of Liberalism, and I refer to the Leader of the Opposition and the even more obsolete and train-catching hon. member for Essex East. For the house is well aware, sir, that the present big guns of Liberalism are that trio of tyros, Gordon, Drury and Sharp, all of whose ideas as presented at the Kingston conference and at the January rally have been repudiated this afternoon by their erstwhile leaders.
Indeed, sir, as I listened with fascination to the Leader of the Opposition the only conclusion I could achieve was that the only consistency of the Leader of the Opposition was his total inconsistency with all previous pronouncements which he has made. That which he and the hon. member for Essex East have previously supported they themselves this afternoon repudiated. That which they have previously attacked they now assert as revealed wisdom.
Throughout the whole afternoon the Leader of the Opposition blew hot and cold. He straddled the fence, indeed, to such an extent that I thought the rust from the barbs of wire would eat right into his soul.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Quotation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: First, I must deal with the pontifications of the hon. member for Essex East on the subject of the automobile industry. Seldom has the house been treated to such skilful evasion as when he was asked what, if any, recommendations of the Bladen report he approved.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which ones do you approve?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He squirmed and he wiggled and he evaded.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You always want to know what we would do but you are the government.

The Budget-Mr. R. A. Bell

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He did everything but answer. He poses as an expert, but what an expert. Even when he was offered unanimous consent to state his opinions to the house he avoided and evaded the whole issue. This should not surprise the house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I did ask for leave of the house to make a second speech but this was denied me and among those who denied me this opportunity was the hon. gentleman who now so unfairly attacks a conscientious member.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, never would I attack the hon. gentleman fairly or unfairly. The hon. member indicated that it would take him 40 minutes to answer a straightforward question which he might have answered in two sentences. He posed and he postured today, and he has on each occasion, as the one responsible for the abolition of the 7J per cent excise tax on motor vehicles.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What a laugh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the record? I want to put that record before the house. According to the Parliamentary Guide, the hon. member for Essex East was sworn in as a cabinet minister on April 18, 1945.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A pretty black day.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: For the following 12 years until the 21st day of June, 1957, he was an integral and very vocal part of the ministry of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He was the whole show.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What happened to the excise tax on automobiles during that time?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was reduced to 15 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, let my hon. friend possess his soul in patience because I will put the complete record on Hansard.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On that black day of April 18, 1945, when the hon. gentleman was sworn in as a minister the excise tax on automobiles was 10 per cent, and on that happy day in 1957 when he ceased to be a minister what was the excise tax?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Ten per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We were selling motor cars in those days.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Yes, 10 per cent. What happened in the meantime? Here is the situation. On the 17th day of November, 1947,
[Mr. Martin (Essex East) .1

which must have been about the time of taxation by radio, what happened to the excise tax? The tax on the first $1,200 of the value of an automobile was raised to 25 per cent and on the next $800 to 50 per cent. On the value of an automobile in excess of $2,000 it was raised to 75 per cent. During that period of time the hon. member was the minister of national health and welfare and he was the member for Essex East professing to represent the automobile industry. Search the pages of Hansard, search the pages of the newspapers and see if the hon. gentleman ever raised his voice in protest against that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question? I was then a member of the government. Was it possible for me to raise in this house a point involving government policy? Will my hon. friend not say, however, that it is generally known that in cabinet I did fight for that industry and for the workers in the automobile industry.

Finally, on the 5th of April, 1955-

The hon. gentleman has been up many times. I am confined to 30 minutes and I should like to deal with two speeches that have been made and have taken at least two hours to make. Finally, on the 5th of April, 1955 the tax was reduced to 10 per cent.
That was the up and down, on again, off again Finnegan attitude that the hon. member for Essex East and his colleagues adopted during the years in which they were in power. How he can have the effrontery in this house now to claim parenthood for the reduction, I do not know. I suggest he stands exposed by his own inconsistency. His failures when in power to represent the interests of the automobile industry are exposed by what I have put on the record for all to see. How different indeed are the attitudes of the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Spencer) and the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Thrasher) who from the very time they came into this chamber have fought in the interests of the automobile industry.
I was interested in hearing the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) speak on the radio and attack the government in sarcastic and scornful tones for not having adopted in full the commercial policy proposals of the
The Budget-Mr. R. A. Bell Bladen report. How very carefully today his deskmate, the hon. member for Essex East, avoided taking any stand. The hon. member for Ottawa West is the official trade critic for the opposition, and his considered statement was that these proposals of far-reaching importance, vital indeed at this sensitive period in our trading history, should have been implemented without any prior consultations with our trading allies or with industry or with management or with unions. Had the government done so without giving such opportunity for consultation, I think the hon. gentleman would have based his attack upon the allegation that we were recklessly jeopardizing our trading relations. What the government has done in this respect is to act responsibility in these far-reaching proposals. I believe the result of this responsible attitude will be generally beneficial to the automobile industry and to the people of Canada as a whole.
Then, Mr. Speaker, what of the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson)? Carefully he avoided most of the significant features of the budget. He talked a great deal of an election. How the very thought of that event must make the hon. gentleman shudder. He was bold in January of 1958 when he challenged this government to an election. Oh, how confident he was on January 20, 1958. What was the result? The result was the decimation of his party. Look at the serried ranks of Liberalism opposite.

speechtext:
The result of that clean sweep was three to one, and three to one it still is.
The whole speech of the Leader of the Opposition I thought was one of the better examples of Lamontagne phrase making but it carefully avoided any stand on any kind of issue, for all issues he evaded and straddled.
Oh, no, there was one thing on which he seemed to get steady. He seemed to get steady on the Arrow. He opposed the new and most satisfactory deal recently made with the

The Budget-Mr. R. A. Bell United States. This house and this country do not agree with the point of view which the hon. gentleman expressed. I believe that is a most satisfactory arrangement and one which will earn the commendation of the people of this country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is just the hon. member's opinion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
