speechtext:
Oh, yes; I took down a phrase, "confusion, indecision and delay". That is what he asserts. He relates that phrase to the most comprehensive, realistic and expansionist budget in our history. That is the test of the hon. gentleman's judgment and of his economic reasoning. He had scorn for the deficit. It is not an expansionist deficit, he said. If it is not an expansionist deficit, what is it? He carefully avoided saying.
On television, as I hear, he very freely admitted that in the unhappy event he had been on the treasury benches this last year, there would have been a deficit and a very large one. Oh, he favours a deficit but not one which is achieved by the far-reaching policies of this government.
As was so carefully pointed out by the Minister of Finance yesterday, there are only two ways in which to avoid a deficit. The first is to reduce expenditures such as expenditures for social justice payments. Does the hon. gentleman wish us to reduce any of these expenditures that this government has increased with respect to the various social justice payments? Does he want us to reduce the payments made to the provinces which this government, in fact, has doubled since 1957? What would he wish us to reduce?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The interest on the debt.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will answer the hon. member's question, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend has had an hour and a half this afternoon. He has had all the time he required and I do not want him to use any of mine.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was only going to answer the question asked by the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I say to the hon. gentleman that at the present time silence for him would not only be golden but unusual.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You are asking a
rhetorical question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do not ask me questions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The second way in which to avoid a deficit is to raise taxes. Does my hon. friend stand with his friend Jim Coyne in favouring a massive increase in taxes? Does he want a 3 per cent increase

in income and corporate taxes? Does he stand for this new national development tax to raise $300 million or $400 million as his friend Mr. Coyne, under the urging of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), now advocates? Does he favour increases in taxes on cigarettes and liquor as Coyne does? Does he stand with Coyne in the matter of increases in taxes or is he against Coyne?
I myself thought the most unusual thing the hon. gentleman said was this. He said the minister has become a prophet of gloom and doom. What a laugh that was. The test of the hon. gentleman's judgment is just in that phrase. This government, on the eve of the 94th birthday of Canada, is filled with confidence in Canada's future and the greatest of hopes and expectations under the progressive and realistic policies of this government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: After being asleep for four years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The predictions of the Minister of Finance, said the Leader of the Opposition, erred on the conservative side. By that I assume he meant that the predictions will be exceeded. What interpretation can the house put on this comment? Surely the only interpretation that it can put on it is that the policies in the budget will have an even more significant and salutary effect or impact upon the economy than that which even the Minister of Finance himself predicted. If that be the case-and what other interpretation can one take from what the Leader of the Opposition said?-then what greater commendation of the budget can there be? I invite the hon. gentleman to support the budget which will be, in his opinion, so satisfactory and as to which the predictions are, as he says, on the conservative side.
Of all the spurious arguments that the hon. gentleman advanced at any time, I thought the most spurious one was that in which he dealt with the Atlantic provinces. Hon. members from the Atlantic provinces will be able to bring the hon. gentleman up to date. They will be able to tell him what this government has done for those provinces in the Atlantic provinces grants and in the increases of $10 million in the latest proposal to the provinces. For 22 years the maritimes were wholly neglected by hon. gentlemen opposite. The advent of this government spelled a new era for the Atlantic provinces. I believe that those provinces will show to my hon. friend just how they have reacted to the sort of treatment they have secured in this new era under this new goverment.
Then the Leader of the Opposition spoke of the exchange on the Canadian dollar. In everything he said I thought he was totally

inconsistent, not only with Walter Gordon but really with himself and with everything that he had previously said on the subject. Indeed, I thought his comments were an almost incredible contradiction of the January Liberal rally. Is he for or against the use of the exchange fund? He did not say. He just straddled the fence. Again he tried to get himself into a position in which, whatever happens, he would have on the record some phrases so that he could say "I told you so". That, I submit to the house, is not the course of statesmanship. The house would admire him more if he would make up his mind, take a stand and "stay put". To get on both sides of every issue is not the approach the Canadian people expect of a responsible political leader.
One might go on indefinitely to speak of the speech of the Leader of the Opposition and of all its contradictions and extravagant exaggerations. However, all I wish to say is this. His conclusions were based upon false premises and each of the premises was contradictory of most of his previous assertions. He said there were conflicting objectives in the budget. I throw that statement back at him. I say that this budget is an integral part of a responsible, cohesive program of fiscal, monetary and commercial policy. I say that it has already made a massive start towards the achievement of its objectives. When this house tomorrow, I hope, makes it possible for us to get the co-operation of the Bank of Canada and to place a strong figure in the position of governor of the Bank of Canada, I believe there will be an even greater spurt towards the achievement of those objectives.
In his final words the hon. gentleman said something about the growth in per capita debt. I have dealt with this matter on other occasions in the house. The hon. gentleman so carefully avoided saying anything about the net per capita debt and about our ability to pay.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Every baby born shares the debt.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, Mr. Speaker, from his seat the hon. gentleman, my old friend from Kenora-Rainy River, keeps mumbling. I confess I cannot hear what he is saying, though what he says occasionally succeeds in getting on Hansard.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I said, every baby born shares the debt.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman would contain himself in silence for a while, it would be appreciated. Yesterday afternoon the Minister of Finance set forth in a table at page 7220 of Hansard the precise position with respect to the net per capita debt; the fact that it is considerably lower today 90205-6-459
The Budget-Mr. R. A. Bell than it was in 1950; that the net debt expressed as a percentage of gross national product has been consistently dropping since this government came into power. Whereas in 1950 the net debt expressed as a percentage of gross national product was 70.7 and in 1956 it was 41.6, today it is 34.6. That, sir, is the real test. It is the test of our capacity to pay. As I mentioned in my earlier speech on the budget, the braintrusters of the hon. gentlemen opposite do not agree in any way with the attitude they have taken.
Obviously this budget cannot be analysed in isolation from other government policies. It does not exist in a vacuum, insulated from the other measures proposed to parliament this session. It is part of a cohesive, integrated, positive program of action designed in a massive way to stimulate production, promote economic recovery, expand employment, develop resources and promote our external trade opportunities. The provisions of the supplementary budget have already had a significant impact on the encouragement of more effective use of Canadian savings in the development of our resources and in the improvement of our balance of payments situation. Decidedly the trends have all been in the right direction, although they have not proceeded far enough.
Our exports in the year 1960 reached the highest point in our history, and what is not too generally known is that our deficit in external commodity trade last year was much less than one quarter of the peak level of 1956, the last full year during which hon. gentlemen opposite occupied the treasury benches.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And the gross national product took the biggest dive we have had since the war.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I again hear some type of remark from my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River. If the hon. gentleman has anything to say, I wish he would rise and say it.

Sir, at this session parliament has enacted legislation to provide new assistance to housing, including urban renewal and slum clearance, loans for university residences, loans and write-off for municipal sewage installations, new and vitally important capital and maintenance aid for vocational training,

The Leader of the Opposition cannot assert, and he has carefully avoided asserting, that there is any other country in the western world which has adopted a program of economic and social action in any way comparable in extent, depth and impact to that which has been presented this session to parliament by this government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why is it the only one that has flopped in the western world?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this budget constitutes part of that program. This budget deserves the support of the house. It deserves, and I believe it will receive, the support of the country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, did you notice that the hon. member who has just spoken is very nervous, as are, I suppose, all Conservative members at the present time? He is almost as nervous as the Conservative members from the province of Quebec.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You would make anybody nervous.

speechtext:

When the hon. member speaks of a three to one victory, I would ask him to bear in mind what I have just said. I think the hon. member is all wrong.
Is he aware that in Kings a Conservative majority of 1,100 has melted to a small majority of 165. Is that the three to one victory referred to by the hon. member who has just spoken? Is he aware that in Esquimalt-Saanich, a Conservative majority of over 14,000 has melted into a small majority of 700?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What do you want-a consolation prize?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would say that if we do not have a general election at this time it is on account of the four by-elections. I am not surprised that the hon. gentleman is very nervous. He even complains because we are using our big guns in order to fight the present budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do you consider yourself a big gun?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is a free democracy. I do not include myself in the big gun category, but I do not think the parliamentary secretary contends that he is a big gun in the Conservative ranks. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now we are getting the blunderbuss.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Why? To defend a bad budget. (Translation) :
Mr. Speaker, let me rather commend the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) for his masterful speech. I am sure the people are only waiting for an opportunity, through a general election, to show their appreciation for the leader of the Liberal party and to take advantage of his competence not in the capacity of Leader of the Opposition, but as prime minister of Canada, to remedy the administration of the present government which has been running the country so badly for four years.
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to commend the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) for his great victory in relation to the budget. In fact, he has been able to persuade the Conservatives to remove the 71 per cent excise tax on cars. However, as he has indicated, this removal of the tax comes too late, because the season is too far advanced.
I understand that the removal of this tax was designed to provide jobs for the unemployed, in view of the unemployment situation created by the Conservative party in the city of Windsor.
It will take more than a year before those unemployed workers can return to their jobs. Had the tax been removed two or three years ago, the citizens of Windsor who are now unemployed would not have to go back to their jobs, because they would already be there, and we would not see in the province of Quebec and in the other provinces the foreign cars which are displacing Canadian cars. Those cars came into Canada

as a result of the trade mission led by the present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill), and it seems that our trade commissioners were less interested in selling Canadian cars than in buying cars abroad.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why did your own party not remove this tax in 1956?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems that this budget is an effort to repair the damage done by the government, but unfortunately, some of the damage will remain. Happily, the Canadian people will not have to wait too long to rid themselves of the present government's sloppy administration.
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to support the position of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), who pointed out the meanness of this government in depriving postal employees of statutory leave.
I also take this opportunity to note the arrival in the house of the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton), who probably heard that I was going to speak; knowing his great fondness for my speeches, I thank him for coming to the house. While he is here, let me say how mean it is to deprive his employees of statutory leave, when employees of private enterprise are allowed such leave.
What is worse, to my mind, is that those who have intermittent employment, that is who do not regularly work eight hours a day, are not even entitled to annual leave. I think such an attitude is inhuman and small-minded.
In the city of Montreal, there are some postal employees who work intermittently seven days a week, and if one of them wants to leave, he must do so at his own cost and expense, because this government does not pay him a single cent. To my mind, such conditions are inhuman and obsolete.
I asked the Postmaster General a question with regard to this matter and he asked me to wait and reiterate my question when his estimates were discussed. All that is very well, but if a general election comes in the meantime, I am very much afraid that I shall not be able to ask him the same question, for the good reason that he will not be Postmaster General any more.
However, I would ask him not to wait until the post office estimates are discussed next year before he considers this request made to him by the hon. member for Skeena, myself and all opposition members, in view of getting fair treatment for these civil servants who are working intermittently.

I do not wish to make any comments as far as the issues are concerned. I wish to ask the Minister of Finance and the government to send some investigators there to watch the inquiry and find out whether there is some way of finding more money, because every year the government has deficits of hundreds of millions of dollars. Is it not the same as far as the hospital is concerned? I think the present government should look into every hospital in the province of Quebec which was administered by the Union Nationale. There is one, for instance, St. Luc hospital. Every director of this hospital is a Union Nationale organizer. I want the Minister of Finance to make inquiries about it. If the minister needs money he should ensure that income tax is paid by all Canadians. It is only just that those who pay their income taxes honestly should be protected. The government should ensure that those who perhaps do not earn their money in the same way most Canadian taxpayers do should also pay income tax.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to take part in the budget debate at this time. Firstly, it gives me the opportunity to indicate my admiration of the wonderful speech made earlier this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in which he dealt with practically all of the items and problems mentioned in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), a week or so ago.
Second, Mr. Speaker, it gives me the opportunity to express the views of the people of Nickel Belt, the riding which I represent, concerning the budget. We all realize that the budget is possibly the criterion on which the government is judged from year to year, and necessarily this budget is no exception.
As I criticize some of the matters contained in the budget I am sure that the people of my area will agree with me. I feel it is my duty to constructively criticize the budget as have so many newspapers throughout the country and as was so ably done this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition who criticized the economic position of Canada at the present time after four years of Conservative administration.
As recently as last night a friend of mine presented me with a very small book which I consider to be possibly one of the oldest books in Canada having to do with trade and economic problems. This book was written in 1811, 150 years ago. It is entitled "Cursory Observations". The author is Jeremy Cockloft, the elder. The person who wrote this book thought that at that time the government was going to the dogs. It contains a chapter which deals with economics and trade. It ends up practically stating that the country should be given away to the states. The last phrase of the chapter reads as follows:
*-hastening the disunion ol the federal government, which already begins to totter on its foundation.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, if this writer was living in 1961 he would have the same remarks to make about the present government. I cannot say that without presenting certain proof and I certainly intend to do that. The Minister of Finance has made it quite clear, as has been repeated in this house, that he felt

that what he was presenting to the country was a planned solution to our problems, and that in effect the deficit which the budget indicated was planned also. I feel, Mr. Speaker, as do most Canadians, that the deficits of this government are not planned. If they are one cannot fail to observe that they recur from year to year.
I asked for and received the amounts of the deficits that have been incurred from year to year since this government has been in office. For the year ended March 1, 1958, the deficit was $38.5 million. For the year ended March 31, 1959, the deficit was $609.5 million; for 1960, the deficit was $413 million; for 1961, $345 million; and the budget just brought down by the minister estimates that for 1962 the deficit will be in the neighbourhood of $650 million. This is definitely not sound planning but it is the type of situation that this government creates from year to year. As indicated, there may be reasons why a government must have a deficit from time to time and with that I very much agree. The last one was poorly planned; perhaps it was not planned at all.
As we go about trying to find reasons for this great deficit at this time we find they do not necessarily relate to questions having to do with the needs of the economy. I am told that possibly the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) gave the clue to the Minister of Finance for the deficit budget which he presented. The Prime Minister appeared on television the day after the presentation of the budget and it might have been expected that as the head of the government he would have indicated the reasons for the deficit. I have a transcript of his television address on June 21, 1961 in which he explained the reasons for the deficit. One thing he said was, "Should we turn back the clock on the Columbia river"?
It would seem that he meant to indicate to the Canadian people that this was a reason for the deficit forecast by the Minister of Finance. We all know that no such project will possibly even be commenced, let alone have to be paid for, before the termination of the year covered by this budget. We all know that the government has got into a shemozzle with one of the provinces with regard to the Columbia river situation.
I am very grateful to those responsible that I was a member of the delegation to Washington recently. In walking the streets there and talking to the American people one found they were very anxious to know what the situation was with respect to the Columbia river. In the minds of our neighbours some fear has possibly been created because we have not confirmed the Columbia river contract. For the sake of expediency and
The Budget-Mr. Godin possibly publicity on the eve of an election in that country, we purported to sign a contract with that country. Surely it is not fitting and right for the Prime Minister of this country to go on the air the day after the budget speech and indicate to the Canadian people that a deficit was required in order to go ahead with such projects which we all realize it will not be possible to commence during the period covered by this budget.
We were told that the deficit was needed to bring about a reduction in taxes with a consequent reduction in revenue to the government from the people, but we have been told by many that this amounts to barely one tenth of 1 per cent of the deficit or approximately $65,000, and the balance must come from other sources and not through any reduction in taxation.
We are told that this deficit is planned. I believe the Leader of the Opposition made reference to that this afternoon. We all recall very well that around Christmas time last year the Canadian tax foundation made an estimate that the deficit in the present budget would be nearly $700 million. Surely the Minister of Finance cannot establish in this house that the tax foundation was planning his budget and his deficit as well.
We are told that one of the main objects of the budget, which is certainly of great importance to Canadian citizens, is to bring about a decrease in interest rates. If there is to be such a large deficit and if the cash position of the government is short, surely the government will have to find the money somewhere. I am quite prepared to admit that I am not a specialist in economics but there are only two ways of obtaining money when you are short of it. Either you borrow the money or you print it. I feel that the government will surely find itself in that position. With such a very large borrower in the field, I cannot conceive of the availability of money not being decreased with the result that interest rates will increase.
Furthermore, I believe I said in the house a couple of years ago that I had read a definition of a Conservative to this effect, that a Conservative is a person who acts hurriedly after thinking for too long a time. I think this is evident from the budget of the Minister of Finance at this time. We realize that the minister has brought down the budget only after the Canadian people had waited a long time for it and after there had been many requests for it by the opposition. In addition, we find some solutions of problems in the budget which have been put forward repeatedly by the Liberal opposition over a long period of time.

The Budget-Mr. Godin
There is, for instance, the reduction in the excise tax on automobiles. We realize that the devaluation of the dollar will be beneficial in some ways to certain phases of our economy but on the other hand it will harm those industries that buy a great deal from our neighbour to the south. The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) made it quite clear this afternoon that he had requested the elimination of the excise tax on automobiles on many occasions. However, the minister has brought this about after he has already been made aware that the premier of the province of Ontario, where most of our automobile industry is located, has seen fit to impose a three per cent sales tax on all goods sold in the province of Ontario.
If the Minister of Finance believes that he is doing a great thing for the automotive industry, he must realize he is very late in doing so. The premier of the province of Ontario is quite friendly with the present government. We recall that during the 1958 election he went about the country with the Prime Minister and stated to the people of Ontario that if they would elect Mr. Diefenbaker he, Mr. Frost would come to Ottawa and get hundreds of millions of dollars for the people of Ontario. It would appear now that the promises made to Mr. Frost at that time were not lived up to because he saw fit some months ago to announce the imposition of a 3 per cent sales tax. That tax will take a great big chunk off the reduction in the excise tax.

United States in connection with the manufacture of automobiles.
I am speaking now, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the purchasers of automobiles in Canada. In this category is included each and every one in my riding as there are no manufacturers in our area. If the dollar is devaluated, we know very well that, in respect of services, the amount the subsidiary companies in the automobile industry in Canada will lose is great. That amount, of course, the purchasers of automobiles in this country will have to meet.
As undoubtedly every person in Canada realizes, it is not by mere accident that the Canadian automobile is absolutely the same in model as the United States automobile. Although the motors are assembled in Canada or are possibly manufactured to a degree in Canada, it is not by a mere coincidence that they happen to be the same as United States motors. Therefore these companies, as well as the bread producers in this country, well realize that they will be paying more for these services, which are a combined service. In paying more for services and materials the Canadian manufacturers will necessarily have to charge more to the Canadian buyers for the same goods which they are now selling.
I say the situation is the same as that in the case of bread. The Minister of Finance can continue to quarrel and to say that this should not be so. However, these companies have accountants who will figure these costs and these costs will be added. Therefore I am quite positive as, I believe, are tne Canadian people, from their understanding of the matter, that this is very close to being a farce when you indicate in one paragraph that you are taking something away while you know very well that practically the entire deduction indicated in that paragraph is taken away absolutely by another paragraph in which you indicate that you will make all efforts to devaluate the dollar to a significant degree. The guess of any other member of this house is as good as mine but "a significant degree" may be very close to the 4J per cent which is left in this instance. Mr. Speaker, like all the other members now in the house, I heard the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin) express his annoyance about the differences of opinion between the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and the governor of the Bank of Canada. He said that the people has been worried over the conflict between those two persons. Let me simply tell him that if this government had been soft enough to implement the policies Mr. Coyne advocated, namely credit restriction and tax increases, the people of Canada would have been doubly worried.

Many views have already been expressed by members on both sides of this house, Mr. Speaker, about the budget speech delivered by the Minister of Finance. Quite naturally, a number of those comments were spoken in a spirit of partisanship which sometimes blinds judgement, particularly when one is left in the cool areas of the opposition. I would prefer to quote the comments of Canadians who are experts on economic matters and who are not necessarily related to any political party.
However, I should like first to pay an unrestricted tribute-for, unlike Mr. Coyne, we do not like restrictions-to the Minister of Finance whose greatest merit is, I humbly submit that of having introduced a budget imbued with great Canadianism and having shown his attachment, for which we congratulate him, to the protection of Canadian business and industries.
It is easy to see how popular the last budget has been by looking through many Canadian newspapers. In fact, one of the best informed papers in Ontario, the Globe and Mail, published in the financial column of Mr. Ronald Anderson a lengthy and favourable comment from which I quote the following:
The budget presented Tuesday by the Hon. Donald Fleming, Minister of Finance, contains three important provisions to help Canadian business. The first and most important one is the plan to reduce the external value of the Canadian dollar: second, the proposal to bring about a decrease in interest rates; third, the abolition of the 7] per cent excise tax on passenger cars.
Those are constructive measures. Other significant proposals provide for the extension of the role and financial resources of the industrial development bank and a tax deduction for research expenditures.
A weekly newspaper highly considered by all businessmen across Canada, the Financial Post, had something in the same line as Mr. Anderson. In last week's issue, the following editorial comment could be found:
The budget contains a host of provisions whose unquestionable usefulness the Canadian people will appreciate. An example of this is the incentive given to research conducted in our country. Another is the extension of the functions and powers of the industrial development bank. It is hoped that this will slow down the selling-off of Canadian business.
And I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this is an important point.
The various steps concerning the bond market are very sound. The provision for a new and thorough study of our financial institutions is timely, and our newspaper has often advocated it. These are all fruitful improvements.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I prefer to rely on the views of experts on financial matters

who are somewhat independent from all political parties, rather than on the views put forward by the hon. gentlemen opposite.
Many businessmen express as much satisfaction as the reporters of the Globe and Mail and the Financial Post. Automobile manufacturers welcome the abolition of the 7J per cent excise tax. Textile manufacturers are glad to be able to count on a greater protection for their products. At this point, I must say that I represent a riding where there is a textile mill; it is therefore with pleasure that the workers of my area welcomed the proposals of the present government.
Exporters are pleased to compute the increased profits they will make from larger sales on the world markets. Hundreds of small businessmen will apply with more confidence to the industrial development bank. Finally, special incentives for the replacement and modernization of equipment will step up production in a great many factories.
The Minister of Finance has efficiently coordinated both monetary and fiscal measures. Some opportunist politicians blame him for it. Those who view the situation as statesmen must-like the members of the committee of the other place-commend him for it. The odds are that the Canadian people will finally come into line with the statesmen.
The people will soon realize that the June 20 budget shows a true Canadian spirit. The case of textiles will prove them right.
In order to show the importance of the textile industry in Canada, I shall simply read part of a speech made last April by the president of the Cotton Institute of Canada and managing director of Hamilton Cotton Limited of Hamilton, Ontario. This is what he said:
The manufacturing industry employs today about 25 per cent of the Canadian labour force, compared to 16 per cent for agriculture, only 5 per cent for our resource industries, and about 30 per cent for service industries, including all sectors of trade and transport. It is a well known fact that the so-called service industries greatly depend on the manufacturing industries. In fact, a recent investigation undertaken by the C.N.R. reveals that each job in the manufacturing industry provides 1.17 jobs in other industries.
Therefore, it is obvious that as far as employment is concerned, it is by helping the largest employer, the manufacturing industry, that we will get the most benefit. Now, the textile industry, of which we are a significant group, is a vital sector of the Canadian manufacturing industry. In fact, the primary textile industry is the country's second most important employer in the manufaetur-90205-6-460J
The Budget-Mr. Lafreniere ing field-the first place being occupied by the wearing apparel industry. Its importance is therefore obvious.
Under the Liberals, the textile industry was treated as a poor relative. It was left to the mercy of foreign competition. The present member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) stated in this house that the textile industry deserves very little consideration because, according to him, it is artificial from three points of view: (1) its skilled labour; (2) its methods; (3) its raw materials.
Unfortunately, those words express only too well the attitude which the Mackenzie King government took with regard to that industry which is such a large employer. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, it is no news for you that the member for Bonavista-Twillingate did not intervene when the customs tariffs which served as a dike against the flooding of our market by imported textile products, were under assault. We had to wait until the Conservatives came to power for the textile industry to recover the protection which is so essential to its survival.
The present Minister of Finance has negotiated agreements under which the Japanese put quotas on their exports to our country. The minister also proposes increases in the tariff rates which should help that industry develop even more. No one will forget that, at least not in the province of Quebec where, not including Montreal, one worker out of seven is in the employ of a textile mill.
I should like here, Mr. Speaker, to quote from a speech made by Mr. Young, president of the Canadian cotton institute, in order to warn the government against the dangers which are involved for this product in the competition from our southern neighbours, the United States. Here is what Mr. Young said:
Since 1956, the United States government has spent nearly $20 million in subsidizing textile goods shipped into Canada. These shipments represent now 45 per cent of the American cotton goods exports and compares with 18 per cent in the carrying out of this program. During the same period, the Canadian cotton textile industry laid off 4,800 employees and, at the end of 1960, it was employing only 17,300 persons.
It is clear that this subsidy is paid to make more business for the American exporters in reducing their export prices.
Consequently, I should like the government to strengthen, if possible, the measures taken to protect our industry against that competition from the United States.

The Budget-Mr. Lafreniere
The June 20 budget shows a true Canadian spirit, as I said, as far as the protection of our foreign markets is concerned. There is every indication that if we can go on selling our raw materials in England, we will have to continue selling our secondary products in the other countries of the commonwealth: India, Australia, New Zealand, the new African states. If we were to press London to join the common market, we would disturb the whole structure of the preferential tariff, we would throw out of key this whole tariff at a time when India and a number of African states, about to enter industrialization, could absorb large quantities of our secondary products.
There is no need to read publications such as Foreign Trade to get a clear indication of the magnitude of our trade with commonwealth countries, and of the possibilities in that field. Any thinking person knows about them. That is why the Minister of Finance could state with his usual firmness:
This historic right of commonwealth free access to the United Kingdom market for agricultural products, industrial material and most manufactured goods is the keystone of the commonwealth trading system. Not only for economic reasons, hut for political reasons as well, we would not wish to see this system abandoned ... We will pursue whatever policies may be required to achieve this end.
Those proud words are in full agreement with the ways in which the Minister of Finance, in international conferences, has stood for the rightful interests of Canadian producers.
After all, if the Minister of Finance has always defended our producers, he has done so by means of structural reforms, to use the words of Mr. Jacques Parizeau, and in referring to those reforms I am led to stress the consistency that any observant person will find in the various budgets introduced by the Minister of Finance. In fact, the June budget is but an extension of the December one. It is its logical outcome.
Have I not referred, a moment ago, to the sound protectionism that the June 20 budget forecasts in the field of textiles? Well, in December, the Minister of Finance had redefined, for customs purposes, products of a class or kind made in Canada. The new definition will have as its essential result to encourage purchasers of machinery to buy their manufacturing equipment in this country. Mr. Jacques Parizeau noted in this connection:
For a long time, the equipment imported into Canada has been segregated by customs authorities under two classifications according to whether it was possible or not for the importer to purchase similar equipment in Canada. In the first instance, tariffs were often from 15 to 25 percent; in the second instance, however, they ranged between nil and 7J per cent. Those provisions have often been evaded in the past and the second classifica-

tion has been rather large compared to the first. Abuse has become general. With a re-definition of those classes, the Minister of Finance in fact has re-defined hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of imports and increased the effective protection of the equipment industry which employs large numbers of workers.
In December last, the Minister of Finance had taken correlated steps to reduce the inflow of imports and favour the Canadians seeking markets abroad for Canadian products. He has provided for the creation of an export bank which offers short and long term credit through the chartered banks. Canadian exporters have benefited from the creation of that bank as of December 1960, as they will benefit from the devaluation of the dollar as of June 20, 1961.
Labour itself has not been ignored either. In December, in order to eliminate unemployment pockets in depressed areas, the Minister of Finance invited business firms to those areas and backed his invitation with generous tax abatements. In June, he has decided to encourage employment in the automobile industry; in fact, he has abolished the 7J per cent excise tax. Because of the automatic reduction of new car prices, demand will increase and production will advance accordingly.
Whether we refer to the main budget or to the baby budget, our findings are the same -the present government pursues the same objectives. Should they be indicated once again?
1.	Balancing our trade through diversification;
2.	Abiding by international commitments, such as GATT and defending our rights and interests;
3.	Protecting our producers against unfair competition in the industrial and agricultural fields.
In view of that threefold aim the government has been trying to rationalize capital inflow. The rate of public and private investments will not be slowed down in the process; there will simply be a substitution of Canadian funds for foreign funds. That is why the Minister of Finance said:
Since our aim is to reduce substantially and fairly quickly our excess of imports, visible and invisible, over our exports, it follows that we must aim at replacing, from Canadian sources, an equivalent amount of funds that would otherwise have been raised abroad. We have been giving most careful thought to ways and means of supplying these funds from Canadian sources.
This cannot happen overnight. For a long time, borrowers in this country have been used to going to New York to raise money. On that world money market, lenders are so easily found that unimaginative borrowers

services, however excellent, of our own financial institutions.
The central government will set an example. Better still, it will take concrete action to ease the long term bond sector available to the provinces and municipal corporations. Therefore, the Minister of Finance announced on June 20:
-I propose to restrict new federal bond issues, at least for many months, to the field of short term securities.
This action is along the same lines as the treasury decision to take over the whole portfolio of the unemployment insurance fund on the basis of the book value of the bonds. To this dual approach should be added the measures taken by the government to open a secondary mortgage market. In June as in December, the government has shown its intention to enlarge and develop the Canadian capital market. Those, Mr. Speaker, are the points on which I wanted to call the attention of the house.
The general idea that one can derive from this budget is that the minister has tried to protect Canadian industry and Canadian companies.
He deserves to be commended for that attitude. It is, indeed, for that reason that every newspaper across the country has spoken favourably of the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance.
Independent and impartial opinions of newspaper columnists and economic experts mean more, in my view, than the more or less sincere opinions which have been expressed by hon. members opposite.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) made his annual fiscal accounting to the Canadian people, there was what purported to be another national accounting made to the people by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). This so-called accounting was made in a television address on the occasion of the fourth anniversary of the mounting to the seats of the mighty by the Conservative party. It is with this latter accounting that I intend to deal for a few moments.
The Prime Minister during his television chat invited Canadians to look over the shadow his administration had cast across Canada under his stewardship. Perhaps more properly I should have said spectre, not
The Budget-Miss LaMarsh shadow. He invited Canadians to join with him in his self-satisfied gloating over the period when, as he said, there had been more development in Canada than in any equal period in the past. Alas, Mr. Speaker, what a sad commentary on the 1957 model man of vision who is now, in 1961, the model man of hallucinations. Is that too strong a word, Mr. Speaker? Surely this is the most charitable explanation of that half hour of half truths which he gave the Canadian people.
This is what he said, Mr. Speaker:
And now, I look back with you over the four years. What have been the effects? The national income has risen 18 per cent and the gross national product-that is all our earnings and income and production-by 17 per cent.
This, Mr. Speaker, so far as it goes-and I say so far as it goes-is the truth. But what he neglected to mention was that during the last four years of Liberal administration, from 1953 to 1957, the national income rose not 18 per cent but 24 per cent and the gross national product during the same period rose not 17 per cent but 27 per cent.
Let me quote what one of the most Conservative of Canadian papers, the Financial Post, said in its editorial "The Spectre of Stagnation" on April 29 last:
What is important about G.N.P., however, is not the sometimes stunning dollar totals and their frequently quoted advances.
What matters to practical business planners and to responsible government officials should be real rates of growth. And here the G.N.P. story reveals the spectre of stagnation.
Consider these comfortless figures:
Since 1947, G.N.P.'s average annual rate of increase has been almost 8 per cent. This, on the surface is a remarkable performance but the average hides the fact that between 1947 and 1956 the annual average was 9 per cent, while in the last four years the rate of increase has been only half as fast-4 per cent per year. To see how small the real volume gains are, take out the effect of price increases. Then the annual 9 per cent gain from 1947 to 1956 turns into a 5.5 per cent advance and the 4 per cent increase 1956- 1960 slows to a 1.7 per cent annual rise.
This, Mr. Speaker, more than shows the hollow puffing of the government, but the most chilling aspect is that if one does take out from the G.N.P. these figures to arrive at the real G.N.P. per person in Canada, without the rise in cost and considering the population increases then in fact in the past four years the G.N.P. per person in Canada has dropped 4 per cent. This means that while under the Liberal administration of 1956 each person produced $96 more, under this government each Canadian produced $55 less.

The Budget-Miss LaMarsh
But to return to the Cheshire cat recital of the Prime Minister of last week, he said at page 7 of the script of his broadcast:
Progress and expansion on the scale of the last four years is not inevitable.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I join with most other Canadians in saying thank heaven that that is so and that it is not inevitable.
Then, as an example of a sheer flight of imagination, listen to what the Prime Minister said on the subject of trade:
And when you think of the doom and gloom remember this, Canadian exports have been steadily increasing since we took office and they're now, 1960-
And I may say this is obviously a speech left over from last year. I continue:
-at an all time high, 12 per cent higher than they were four years ago.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that during the last four years of Liberal administration trade in Canada increased by almost the same figure; actually it was somewhat higher, 12.8 per cent. But in the past four years world trade has expanded 20 per cent. Canada has slipped from fourth to fifth place among the world's trading nations.
Then, the Prime Minister took great glee in the drop of 4 per cent in imports, although he was silent on the fact that this is used as a first indication by economists of a drop, and a considerable drop, in personal incomes.
We come now to that part of the Prime Minister's speech where he dealt with the problem of unemployment in Canada, a subject to which perhaps he felt he could at last refer, with the summer season here and people re-employed in the tourist and construction industries. The Prime Minister said:
We have unemployment, the result of men being displaced by technological change.
The Senate committee found a number of reasons for the amount of unemployment in this country but certainly did not dismiss it, as did the Prime Minister, as being merely the result of technological change. Listen to what the Financial Post had to say about the cause of unemployment in the same editorial to which I made reference a while ago.
The result of this trend toward stagnation has been the worst unemployment recession since the 1930's. Unemployment is now averaging 7 per cent a year as against only 2-3 per cent in the early 1950's.
Then the Prime Minister said:
However, in Canada, and it's well to remember this, unemployment has lesser impact on the Canadian than on the American economy. Compare our situation with the United States and then think of this.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe the purpose of this amendment was fully explained in the budget speech. This explanation is to be found at page 6662 of Hansard.
This resolution would have the effect that, in future, cigarettes may weigh as much as three pounds per thousand cigarettes before becoming subject to the higher rate of excise duty. At present the act provides an excise duty of $4 per thousand cigarettes weighing not more than 2J pounds per thousand. If cigarettes weigh more than this limit, the duty is $5 per thousand. This resolution proposes that the point at which the higher rate becomes effective be increased to three pounds per thousand cigarettes. This change will permit manufacturers to put more tobacco in cigarettes than at present without paying higher duty. At the present time most cigarettes longer than normal in size made in Canada are longer because of the filter and are not true "king size" cigarettes as they are known in the United States.
The proposed change will permit the manufacture of so-called "king size" cigarettes without additional tax. It has been estimated by some cigarette manufacturers that this

change may result in the use of an additional ten million pounds of tobacco per year. This is an increase of 8 per cent or 9 per cent in tobacco consumption. Although the change is a tax reduction in that a larger quantity of tobacco may be purchased for the same amount of tax, it is not anticipated the tax revenue will be affected to any significant extent since people purchase cigarettes by number rather than by weight.

Mr. Chairman, for many years subsection 2 of section 3 of the Customs Tariff has provided that the benefits of Canada's British preferential tariff shall apply to goods the growth, produce or manufacture of a specified list of British countries "when conveyed without transshipment from a port of any British country enjoying the benefits of the British preferential tariff into

Customs Tariff
a sea, lake or river port of Canada". Similar language appears also in subsections 1 and 2 of section 5. At the time they were introduced, the words "sea, lake or river" in fact covered all ports to which it was physically possible for goods to be shipped direct from British preferential sources. Such goods had to move by vessel. Hence the phrase "sea, lake or river" was all-inclusive. However, with the development of trans-Atlantic, trans-Pacific, and trans-polar air travel, including cargo movements by air, the strict application of the limiting words "sea, lake or river" would now impose an unintended and undesirable restriction. It would exclude from British preferential treatment any goods arriving by air at some airports in Canada. Accordingly, in order to make it clear that goods shipped direct from a British preferential source to a Canadian airport are not excluded from British preferential tariff treatment, it is proposed to amend the provisions in question.

It was not necessary to provide any compensation outside the textile field in order to conclude negotiations with them. In other words, the countries concerned were satisfied that this represents a balance-the quids and the quos as recommended by the tariff board. As a matter of fact, they were so fully satisfied with the reductions recommended by the tariff board that they were not only prepared to agree to the increases recommended by the tariff board but to forgo in three respects benefits they might have expected to receive under the recommendations of the tariff board. It is clear, therefore, that resolution No. 2 is, as I have said, a balanced package which in its result involves neither higher nor lower tariffs.
There are, of course, gains from the adoption of a more logical and orderly nomenclature and arrangement of items recommended by the board. I think that all parties should benefit from this. Moreover, as I mentioned in the budget speech, the resolutions which I have introduced propose certain departures from the tariff board's recommendations, which will provide somewhat more protection for the knit goods and narrow fabrics sectors of the industry than they otherwise would have had.
As to the four departures which I have mentioned, three involve changes which were requested by Canadian textile producers, while the fourth was introduced in the course of negotiations as a result of representations made by Italy. The three departures recommended by Canadian textile producers concerned, first, knitted goods under item 568; second, socks and stockings other than wool, item 568a(2); and third, narrow fabrics of man-made fibres, item 562a(2). The fourth item which, as I have said, was the occasion of representations by Italy, concerned travel rugs under item 534a(2). I shall make this comment on the last, or fourth item, that the departure in this case from the recommendation of the tariff board involves a downward modification in a rate recommended by the tariff board. This was introduced in the course of negotiations in order to meet a special problem in our trade with Italy. The board recommended that the new tariff item for blankets, item 534(a), include travel rugs as well as household blankets. The composite m.f.n. rate of 20 per cent and 15 cents per pound provided for on this item would have

increased the effective rate on low-priced Italian travel rugs from 27J per cent to about 45 per cent. Italy requested that a ceiling of 37 i per cent be introduced for travel rugs, and a settlement was reached on that basis.
In addition, there are a few minor nonsubstantive changes in wording or arrangement. Those have been introduced for technical reasons or for purposes of clarification.

goods industry, however, the government decided that on balance it would not be desirable to introduce this tariff reduction at this time.

speechtext: I wonder whether the house leader could indicate what the business will be for the rest of the week and, if possible, as has been the custom in the past, indicate the business for next week.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not possible to carry on the custom which we have been following over the last two years, and to indicate the business for next week. The hope of the house, of course, is that we can finish the essential items that are in front of us as quickly as possible. However, I think it is wiser to announce the business from day to day. Tomorrow we will carry on with the resolutions following the budget.

I assume the minister meant what he said, namely that he hoped to get through all the essential business. It would appear to me that there might be a considerable probability that the budget resolutions would not take all of tomorrow. Surely the government has some other business.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Nothing pleases me more than does the request of the house for more business for tomorrow. We have on the order paper Bill No. S-28, to amend the Trust Companies Act.
Surely that is not essential business. That was not in the Prime Minister's list.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: These have been through the house and then over to the other place. Then there is Bill No. S-29 to amend the Loan Companies Act. Then there is the resolution in the name of the Minister of Finance dealing with the Industrial Development Bank Act.
And after that what is there? We are seeking to expedite the business of the house and we should like to have enough business to take a whole day.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We fully appreciate that. There is the resolution in the name of the Minister of Transport in connection with the Pine Point railway which also could be considered.
Is that one of the items the Prime Minister indicated was essential?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No.
Would the minister say whether this program will go on for Saturday as well or could he indicate what would be happening on Saturday?
Will estimates be taken on Saturday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No. The intention will be to complete, in so far as we can, the resolutions and the bills following the budget. If the house passes the resolutions tomorrow, as has now been indicated, then of course, I think the bills would normally follow on Saturday.

On that point, if I may do
so, I think I should say this. Since we are seeking to expedite the closing of the session or the adjournment, whichever it is, I would suggest this to the minister. I do not believe that, in all the period during which I have observed parliament it has ever been customary to take budget bills immediately after the resolutions. There has always been at least an interval of a full day in order to give the opposition a full opportunity to consider the debate on the resolution stage. I suggest that much greater progress would be made if the government did not seek to depart from that usual convention and would find some other business for Saturday.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
For Saturday, and the bills on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: These useful suggestions will be taken into consideration and an announcement will be made tomorrow.
There is no question that it is the intention of the government to have the house sit on Saturday, notwithstanding the fact that it is July 1?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: In the past we have frequently sat on July 1.
Quite so. We are not objecting.
